A Diagram-Like Basis for the Multiset Partition Algebra
Alexander Wilson

Abstract




Abstract
There is a classical connection between the representation theory of the symmetric group and the general linear group called Schur-Weyl duality. Variations on this principle yield analogous connections between the symmetric group and other objects such as the partition algebra and more recently the multiset partition algebra. The partition algebra has a well-known basis indexed by graph-theoretic diagrams which allows the multiplication in the algebra to be understood visually as combinations of these diagrams. We construct an analogous basis for the multiset partition algebra called the diagram-like basis and use this basis to construct its irreducible representations and give a generating set. We also provide a change-of-basis formula from the orbit basis of the multiset partition algebra to this diagram-like basis which exhibits similarities to the analogous change-of-basis formula for the partition algebra.

1.
Introduction

Let
V_{n}
be an
n
-dimensional vector space, and write
{V_{n}}^{\otimes r}
for its
r
th tensor power. The general linear group
GL_{n}
acts on the tensor power diagonally, where a matrix
M\in GL_{n}
acts on each tensor factor:

M.(v_{1}\otimes\dots\otimes v_{r})=(Mv_{1})\otimes\dots\otimes(Mv_{r}).

The symmetric group
\mathfrak{S}_{r}
acts on the tensor power by permuting tensor factors:

\sigma\cdot(v_{1}\otimes\dots\otimes v_{r})=v_{\sigma^{-1}(1)}\otimes\dots\otimes v_{\sigma^{-1}(r)}.

These two actions are mutual centralizers. That is, taking the endomorphisms of
{V_{n}}^{\otimes r}
that commute with one action recovers the other. This is an example of Schur-Weyl duality, and one consequence of such a duality is the decomposition

{V_{n}}^{\otimes r}\cong\bigoplus_{\lambda}W_{GL_{n}}^{\lambda}\otimes W_{\mathfrak{S}_{r}}^{\lambda}

where for a group or algebra
A
, we write
W_{A}^{\lambda}
to represent an irreducible representation of
A
and the sum is over partitions
\lambda
of
r
. This establishes a correspondence between irreducible
GL_{n}
-modules and irreducible
\mathfrak{S}_{r}
-modules and allows information to be passed between the representation theory of the two groups.

Any situation in which two actions mutually centralize each other leads to an analogous decomposition. The study of these centralizer algebras is connected to long-standing questions in the representation theory of the symmetric group and
GL_{n}
including the Kronecker problem
[
BDVO15
,
OZ23
]
, the restriction problem, and plethysm
[
OSSZ22
]
.

For another example, let
V_{n,k}=(\mathbb{C}^{n})^{k}
be the space of
n\times k
matrices and let
\mathcal{P}^{r}(V_{n,k})
be the space of polynomial forms on
V_{n,k}
. The group
GL_{n}
naturally acts on
V_{n,k}
by left-multiplication. This action extends to
\mathcal{P}^{r}(V_{n,k})
where
M\in GL_{n}
acts on
f(X)\in\mathcal{P}^{r}(V_{n,k})
by

(M.f)(X)=f(M^{-1}X).

The group
GL_{k}
can act analogously where
N\in GL_{k}
acts by:

(N.f)(X)=f(XN).

In
[
How95
]
, Roger Howe determined that these actions are mutual centralizers leading to a decomposition

\mathcal{P}^{r}(V_{n,k})\cong\bigoplus_{\lambda}W_{GL_{n}}^{\lambda}\otimes W_{GL_{k}}^{\lambda}

where the sum is over partitions
\lambda
of
r
of length at most
\min\{n,k\}
(see e.g. Section 5.2.6 of
[
GW09
]
for details).

In the 1990’s, Martin
[
Mar94
]
introduced the partition algebra
P_{r}(n)
as a generalization of the Temperley-Lieb algebra and the Potts model in statistical mechanics. In the case that
n\geq 2r
, the partition algebra is the algebra whose action centralizers the action of
\mathfrak{S}_{n}\subseteq GL_{n}
as the subgroup of permutation matrices acting on
{V_{n}}^{\otimes r}

[
Jon94
,
Mar91
,
MS94
]
. From this perspective, there is a natural basis for
P_{r}(n)
called the orbit basis, but its product is complicated. A second basis called the diagram basis has a much simpler product in terms of graph-theoretic diagrams. The partition algebra, its generators, and its representations have been well-studied, and some major milestones are outlined in the following timeline.

Partition algebra
introduced with
orbit and diagram basis
[
Jon94
,
Mar91
]
Partition algebra
shown to be cellular
[
Xi99
]
(small correction in
[
GP18
]
)
Presentations by generators
and relations given
1
1

1

Other notable presentations for
P_{r}(n)
are given in
[
Eas11
,
Eny13a
]
[
HR05
]
Dimensions of irreducibles
described via tableaux
2
2

2

Note that once the cellularity and semisimplicity of
P_{r}(n)
were established, the dimensions of the irreducibles are encoded in the cellular data. However, these papers were the first to describe these dimensions explicitly in terms of tableaux
[
BH19a
,
BH19c
,
OZ21
]
Irreducible
representations
constructed
[
Hal20
,
HJ20
]

A major motivation for studying the partition algebra is to understand its representations and use them to study objects in the representation theory of the symmetric group such as the Kronecker coefficients
[
BH19a
,
BH19c
,
BHH17
,
BDVE21
,
Eny13b
,
Hal01
,
HL06
,
Hal20
]
.

In
[
OZ23
]
, the authors Orellana and Zabrocki restrict the
GL_{n}
action of Howe duality to the
n\times n
permutation matrices to obtain the multiset partition algebra
{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n)
and provide a basis analogous to the orbit basis for
P_{r}(n)
. In
[
OZ20
,
OZ23
]
Orellana and Zabrocki use symmetric function methods to compute the dimensions of irreducible
{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n)
as counting the number of semistandard multiset partition tableaux. Our aim in this paper is to fill in three gaps in the timeline for
{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n)
by:

(a)

providing a basis analogous to the diagram basis for
P_{r}(n)
,

(b)

providing generators for
{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n)
, and

(c)

constructing the irreducible representations of
{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n)
as actions on the tableaux enumeratively predicted by Orellana and Zabrocki.

In
[
NPS23
]
, the authors investigate the centralizer
\End_{\mathfrak{S}_{n}}(\mathcal{P}^{{\boldsymbol{a}}_{1}}(V_{n})\otimes\dots\otimes\mathcal{P}^{{\boldsymbol{a}}_{k}}(V_{n}))
for a weak composition
{\boldsymbol{a}}
of
r
of length
k
, also dubbing it the multiset partition algebra, written
{\rm M\!P\!}_{\boldsymbol{a}}(n)
. Orellana and Zabrocki state that
{\rm M\!P\!}_{\boldsymbol{a}}(n)
should be isomorphic to a subalgebra of their multiset partition algebra, and in this paper we describe that isomorphic subalgebra.

In Section
2
, we define the relevant combinatorial objects and introduce the partition algebra and multiset partition algebra. In Section
3
, we collect some useful facts about orbits of the combinatorial objects under the action of Young subgroups. In Section
4
, we describe the centralizer of an algebra
A
acting on a direct sum of projections of a semisimple module
V
by idempotents. We then construct the irreducible modules over this centralizer in terms of irreducible modules of
\End_{A}(V)
. In the following two sections, we specialize these constructions to the setting of the multiset partition algebra. In Section
5
, we use a decomposition of
\mathcal{P}^{r}(V_{n,k})
as a
GL_{n}
-module to obtain the diagram-like basis and describe
\End_{G}(\mathcal{P}^{r}(V_{n,k}))
for general subgroups
G
of
GL_{n}
. In Section
6
, we construct the irreducible representations of
{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n)
with bases indexed by multiset-valued tableaux. In Section
7
, we provide a generating set for
{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n)
, and finally in Section
8
we provide a change-of-basis formula from the orbit basis of Orellana and Zabrocki to our diagram-like basis.

2.
Preliminaries and Definitions

2.1.
Set and Multiset Partitions

A
set partition

\rho
of a set
S
is a set of nonempty subsets of
S
called
blocks
whose disjoint union is
S
. We write
\ell(\rho)
for the number of blocks in
\rho
. We define
[r]=\{1,\dots,r\}
the
unbarred
numbers and
\left[\bar{r}\right]=\{\bar{1},\dots,\bar{r}\}
the
barred
numbers. We write
\Pi_{2(r)}
for the set of set partitions of
[r]\cup\left[\bar{r}\right]
. For a set
R
and a set partition
\rho
of
S
, write
\rho|_{R}
for the set partition obtained by restricting the elements in
\rho
to only the elements appearing in
R
.

Example 2.1
.

A set partition and its restriction to a set:

\displaystyle\pi

\displaystyle=\{\{1,3\},\{2,4,\bar{1},\bar{2}\},\{\bar{3},\bar{4}\}\}\in\Pi_{2(4)}

\displaystyle\pi|_{[4]}

\displaystyle=\{\{1,3\},\{2,4\}\}

A
weak composition
of an integer
r
of length
k
is a sequence of
k
non-negative integers which sum to
r
. Write
W_{r,k}
for the set of weak compositions of
r
of length
k
. For
{\boldsymbol{a}}\in W_{r,k}
, write
{\boldsymbol{a}}_{i}
for the
i
th number in the sequence.

A
multiset
of size
r
from a set
S
is a finite collection of
r
unordered elements of
S
which can be repeated. We will write multisets in
\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{,\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}
to differentiate them from sets and we will usually denote them by a capital letter with a tilde. We may write multisets using exponential notation
{\tilde{S}}=\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{{s_{1}}^{m_{1}},\dots,{s_{k}}^{m_{k}}\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}
where the multiplicity of the element
s_{i}
is given by the exponent
m_{i}
. We write
m_{s_{i}}({\tilde{S}})=m_{i}
for this multiplicity. Given multisets
{\tilde{S}}=\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{{s_{1}}^{m_{1}},\dots,{s_{k}}^{m_{k}}\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}
and
{\tilde{R}}=\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{{s_{1}}^{n_{1}},\dots,{s_{k}}^{n_{k}}\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}
, write
{\tilde{S}}\uplus{\tilde{R}}=\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{{s_{1}}^{m_{1}+n_{1}},\dots,{s_{k}}^{m_{k}+n_{k}}\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}
for the union of the two multisets.

A
multiset partition

\tilde{\rho}
of a multiset
{\tilde{S}}
is a multiset of multisets called blocks whose union is
{\tilde{S}}
. We write
\ell(\tilde{\rho})
for the number of blocks. Write
\tilde{\Pi}_{2(r),k}
for the set of multiset partitions with
r
elements from
[k]
and
r
elements from
\left[\bar{k}\right]
. For
{\tilde{\rho}}
a multiset partition and
R
a set, write
{\tilde{\rho}}|_{R}
for the multiset partition obtained by restricting the elements in
{\tilde{\rho}}
to only the elements appearing in
R
.

Example 2.2
.

A multiset partition and its restriction to a set:

\displaystyle{\tilde{\pi}}

\displaystyle=\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{1,\bar{1},\bar{1}\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\},\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{1,2,\bar{2}\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}\in\tilde{\Pi}_{2(3),2}

\displaystyle{\tilde{\pi}}|_{\left[\bar{2}\right]}

\displaystyle=\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{\bar{1},\bar{1}\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\},\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{\bar{2}\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}

Finally, we define partial orders on multisets and multiset partitions, which restrict to sets and set partitions as a special case. Let
{\tilde{S}}
and
{\tilde{R}}
be multisets from
[k]
. We say that
{\tilde{S}}<{\tilde{R}}
if one of the following conditions hold: (i)
{\tilde{S}}
is empty and
{\tilde{R}}
is not, (ii)
\max({\tilde{S}})<\max({\tilde{R}})
, or (iii)
\max({\tilde{S}})=\max({\tilde{R}})=m
and
{\tilde{S}}\smallsetminus\{m\}<{\tilde{R}}\smallsetminus\{m\}
. We call this the
last-letter order
on multisets.

Example 2.3
.

Comparisons of multisets:

\displaystyle\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{1,3\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}

\displaystyle\leq\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{1,1,3\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}

\displaystyle\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{1,1,1,2\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}

\displaystyle\leq\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{3\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}

If
{\tilde{\nu}}=\{{\tilde{S}}_{1},\dots,{\tilde{S}}_{k}\}
and
{\tilde{\pi}}=\{{\tilde{R}}_{1},\dots,{\tilde{R}}_{\ell}\}
are multiset partitions, we say that
{\tilde{\nu}}\leq{\tilde{\pi}}
, or
{\tilde{\nu}}
is
coarser
than
{\tilde{\pi}}
, if
{\tilde{\nu}}
can be obtained by combining blocks of
{\tilde{\pi}}
. Precisely, there exists a set partition
\{C_{1},\dots,C_{k}\}
of
[\ell]
so that
\tilde{S}_{i}=\biguplus_{j\in C_{i}}\tilde{R}_{j}
for all
i
.

Example 2.4
.

An example of comparing two multiset partitions:

\displaystyle\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{1,1,3,3\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\},\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{2,3\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}

\displaystyle\leq\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{1,3\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\},\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{1,3\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\},\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{2\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\},\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{3\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}

2.2.
Set and Multiset Partition Diagrams

For a set partition
\pi\in\Pi_{2(r)}
, there is a classical graph-theoretic representation of
\pi
on two rows of vertices with the top row being labeled
1
through
r
and the bottom being labeled
\bar{1}
through
\bar{r}
. Two vertices of this graph are in the same connected component if and only if their labels are in the same block of
\pi
.

Example 2.5
.

The set partition
\pi=\{\{1,\bar{1},\bar{2},\bar{3}\},\{2,3\},\{\bar{4}\},\{4,5,\bar{5}\}\}
could be represented by either of the following two graphs.

Note that there could be many such graphs that represent the set partition
\pi
, so we consider two graphs equivalent if their connected components give rise to the same set partition. The
diagram
of
\pi
is the equivalence class of graphs with the same connected components.

We can similarly consider a graph-theoretic representation of any multiset partition
{\tilde{\pi}}\in\tilde{\Pi}_{2(r),k}
. This time we place
r
vertices on the top labeled by the unbarred elements of the blocks of
{\tilde{\pi}}
in weakly increasing order and place
r
vertices on the bottom labeled by the barred elements in weakly increasing order. We then connect the vertices in any way so that the labeled connected components taken together are
{\tilde{\pi}}
.

Example 2.6
.

The multiset partition
{\tilde{\pi}}=\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{1,\bar{1},\bar{1},\bar{2}\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\},\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{1,1\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\},\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{\bar{2}\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\},\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{2,2,\bar{2}\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}
could be represented by any of the following graphs.

Again we may have many graphs representing the same multiset partition. The
diagram
of
{\tilde{\pi}}
is the equivalence class of graphs whose labeled connected components give
{\tilde{\pi}}
.

We will often drop the labels on these graphs. A set partition diagram will be distinguished by the black color of its vertices, and it will be understood that the vertices are labeled in increasing order left-to-right. A multiset partition diagram will be distinguished by its colored vertices. Its vertices are understood to be labeled with
blue
,
orange
,
green
, and
purple
representing 1, 2, 3, and 4 respectively.

Because of this graphical representation, for a set
S
with elements from
[r]\cup\left[\bar{r}\right]
we will sometimes refer to elements at the “top” of
S
to mean the unbarred elements and elements at the “bottom” of
S
to mean the barred elements, and likewise with multisets.

2.3.
Tableaux

A
partition
of
n
is a weakly-decreasing sequence
\lambda
of positive integers called parts which sum to
n
. We write
\ell(\lambda)
for the number of parts of
\lambda
. We will write
\lambda\vdash n
to mean that
\lambda
is a partition of
n
and write
|\lambda|=n
. Write
\lambda_{i}
for the
i
th element of the sequence
\lambda
, called the
i
th part of
\lambda
, and
{\color[rgb]{0.7695,0.2813,0}\lambda^{*}}
for the partition
(\lambda_{2},\dots,\lambda_{\ell})
obtained by removing the first part. Given a partition
\lambda
, its
Young diagram
is an array of left-justified boxes where the
i
th row from the bottom has
\lambda_{i}
boxes.

When we refer to the
i
th row of a Young diagram, we mean the
i
th row from the bottom, which corresponds to the
i
th part of
\lambda
.

A
tableau
of shape
\lambda
will be a filling of these boxes in
\lambda
’s Young diagram with mathematical objects—in this paper the objects will be positive integers, sets, or multisets. We will call these integer-valued, set-valued, and multiset-valued tableaux respectively. We take a moment to define some particular classes of tableaux.

Let
\rho
be a set partition of
[r]
and
\lambda\vdash n
such that
|\lambda^{*}|\leq\ell(\rho)
. A
set partition tableau
of shape
\lambda
and content
\rho
is a filling
T
of the Young diagram of
\lambda
with the blocks of
\rho
along with
n-\ell(\rho)
empty boxes in the first row. A
standard set partition tableau
is a set partition tableau whose rows increase left-to-right and columns increase bottom-to-top with respect to the last-letter order. Write
\mathcal{SPT}_{\lambda,r}
for the set of set partition tableaux of shape
\lambda
with content a set partition of
[r]
and write
\mathcal{SSPT}_{\lambda,r}
for the subset of
\mathcal{SPT}_{\lambda,r}
consisting of standard set partition tableaux.

Write
\Lambda^{P_{r}(n)}
for the set of
\lambda
for which
\mathcal{SSPT}_{\lambda,r}\neq\emptyset
(we choose this notation because
\Lambda^{P_{r}(n)}
will also be an indexing set for the irreducible
P_{r}(n)
-modules).

Let
\tilde{\rho}
be a multiset partition from
[k]
and
\lambda\vdash n
such that
|\lambda^{*}|\leq\ell(\tilde{\rho})
. A
multiset partition tableau
of shape
\lambda
and content
\tilde{\rho}
is a filling
\tilde{T}
of the Young diagram with the blocks of
\tilde{\rho}
along with
n-\ell(\tilde{\rho})
empty boxes in the first row. A
semistandard multiset partition tableau
is a multiset partition tableau that strictly increases along columns and weakly increases along rows under the last-letter order. Write
\mathcal{MPT}_{\lambda,r,k}
for the set of multiset partition tableaux of shape
\lambda
with content a multiset partition from
[k]
with a total of
r
numbers. Write
\mathcal{SSMPT}_{\lambda,r,k}
for the subset of
\mathcal{MPT}_{\lambda,r,k}
consisting of semistandard multiset partition tableaux.

Remark 2.10
.

We conclude this section on tableaux with two comments regarding the empty boxes. Note that, except for these empty boxes, the standard set partition tableaux and the semistandard multiset partition tableaux closely analogize standard Young tableaux (where each number in
[n]
is used once) and semistandard Young tableaux (where repetition is allowed) respectively. Additionally, for reasons discussed in Section
2.5
, we will usually assume that
n\geq 2r
. In this case, the number of empty boxes in a tableau will always be at least the number of boxes in its second row.

2.4.
Double-Centralizer Theorem

The algebras of interest in this paper arise as the algebras of endomorphisms of
\mathfrak{S}_{n}
-modules, commonly called
centralizer algebras
of
\mathfrak{S}_{n}
. The following theorem summarizes a general case encompassing the Schur-Weyl duality and Howe duality discussed in the introduction as well as the duality between
\mathfrak{S}_{n}
and its centralizer algebras.

Theorem 2.11
.

[
Pro07
, Section 6.2.5]
[
GW09
, Section 4.2.1]
Let
A
be a semisimple algebra acting faithfully on a module
V
and set
B=\End_{A}(V)
. Then
B
is semisimple and
\End_{B}(V)\cong A
. Furthermore, there is a set
P
(a subset of the indexing set of the irreducible representations of
A
) such that for each
x\in P
,
W_{A}^{x}
is an irreducible
A
-module occurring in the decomposition of
V
as an
A
-module. If we set
W_{B}^{x}=\Hom(W_{A}^{x},V)
, then
W_{B}^{x}
is an irreducible
B
-module and the decomposition of
V
as an
A\times B
-module is

V\cong\bigoplus_{x\in P}W_{A}^{x}\otimes W_{B}^{x}.

Moreover, the dimension of
W_{A}^{x}
is equal to the multiplicity of
W_{B}^{x}
in
V
as a
B
-module and the dimension of
W_{B}^{x}
is equal to the multiplicity of
W_{A}^{x}
in
V
as an
A
-module.

The decomposition in the above theorem gives a correspondence between irreducible representations of the algebras
A
and
B
and allows information like dimensions and multiplicities to be passed between them. In this paper, we are interested in setting
A=\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{S}_{n}
. In this case, the indexing set
P
for the irreducible representations is a subset of the integer partitions of
n
.

2.5.
Partition Algebra

For
r
a positive integer and an indeterminate
x
, the partition algebra
P_{r}(x)
is an associative algebra over
\mathbb{C}(x)
first introduced as a generalization of the Temperley-Lieb algebra and the Potts model in statistical mechanics by Jones
[
Jon94
]
and Martin
[
Mar94
,
MS94
]
. When
x
is specialized to an integer
n\geq 2r
, the algebra
P_{r}(n)
is isomorphic to the algebra of endomorphisms
\End_{\mathfrak{S}_{n}}({V_{n}}^{\otimes r})
. The partition algebra has two distinguished bases: the
orbit basis

\{\mathcal{T}_{\pi}:\pi\in\Pi_{2(r)}\}
which arises naturally from the structure of
P_{r}(n)
as a centralizer algebra and the
diagram basis

\{\mathcal{L}_{\pi}:\pi\in\Pi_{2(r)}\}
whose product has a combinatorial interpretation in terms of partition diagrams. The change-of-basis formula is obtained by summing over coarsenings of a diagram:

\mathcal{L}_{\pi}=\sum_{\nu\leq\pi}\mathcal{T}_{\nu}.

The product formula for
\mathcal{L}_{\pi}
can be stated in terms of diagrams as follows. To compute the product of
\mathcal{L}_{\pi}
and
\mathcal{L}_{\nu}
, place a graph representing
\pi
above one representing
\nu
and identify the vertices on the bottom of
\pi
with the corresponding vertices of
\nu
to create a three-tiered diagram. Let
\gamma
be the restriction of this diagram to the very top and very bottom, preserving which vertices are connected and let
c(\pi,\nu)
be the number of components entirely in the middle of the three-tier diagram. Then
\mathcal{L}_{\pi}\mathcal{L}_{\nu}=n^{c(\pi,\nu)}\mathcal{L}_{\gamma}
.

.

In
[
HJ20
]
, the authors construct the irreducible representations
P_{r}^{\lambda}
of
P_{r}(n)
for
n\geq 2r
as a combinatorial action of the set partition diagrams on set partition tableaux. For
\lambda\in\Lambda^{P_{r}(n)}
, the module
P_{r}^{\lambda}
is
\mathbb{C}\{v_{T}:T\in\mathcal{SSPT}_{\lambda,r}\}
with action given as follows. For a set partition
\pi\in\Pi_{2(r)}
to act on a tableau
T
, first pull out the content of
T
, a set partition of
[r]
, into a single row. Then, put
\pi
on top of this row and identify the corresponding vertices. Form
T^{\prime}
by replacing the content of each box in
T
with the set of vertices atop
\pi
that the box is connected to, and for each block entirely in the top of
\pi
, include it as the content of a box in the first row of
T^{\prime}
. If two blocks above the first row are combined or the content of a box does not connect to the top of the partition diagram, the result is zero.

Example 2.13
.

To illustrate the action, we show three examples of different diagrams acting on the same tableau. In the first example, the blocks
4
and
5
can be combined without resulting in zero because one of them is in the first row.

, so the result is zero.

\displaystyle=0

In the following example, the conents of the boxes containing
12
and
3
become connected, so the result is zero.

3

12

4

5

\displaystyle=0

The result
T
of the above process may not be a standard set partition tableau, so we need to make sense of what it means to write
v_{T}
for
T
nonstandard. The algorithm for writing
v_{T}
as a linear combination of standard tableaux is called the
straightening algorithm
. The straightening algorithm for
P_{r}^{\lambda}
is the same as for the Specht modules of
\mathfrak{S}_{n}
applied to the rows above the first row of
T
, a complete treatment of which can be found in
[
Sag01
]
, but we summarize some key features that will be important for our constructions. Given
T\in\mathcal{SPT}_{\lambda,r}
nonstandard, the straightening algorithm writes
v_{T}
as a linear combination

v_{T}=\sum_{S\in\mathcal{SSPT}_{\lambda,r}}c_{S}v_{S}

for some coefficients
c_{S}.

The relations between the
v_{T}
are called Garnir relations and are generally complicated, but one special case will be particularly useful to us: if
T^{\prime}
is the result of exchanging two boxes of
T
above the first row that sit in the same column, then
v_{T^{\prime}}=-v_{T}
.

2.6.
Multiset Partition Algebra

The multiset partition algebra naturally arises by restricting the action of
GL_{n}
on
\mathcal{P}^{r}(V_{n,k})
in Howe duality to the permutation matrices. One can think of elements in
\mathcal{P}^{r}(V_{n,k})
as homogeneous polynomials of degree
r
in indeterminates
x_{ij}
for
1\leq i\leq n
and
1\leq j\leq k
. The action of
GL_{n}
on the space
\mathcal{P}^{r}(V_{n,k})
can be described on monomials as follows. Given a matrix
M=(m_{ij})\in GL_{n}
, its inverse acts on an element of
U_{\boldsymbol{a}}
as follows:

\displaystyle M^{-1}.x_{ij}

\displaystyle=\sum_{\ell=1}^{n}m_{i\ell}x_{\ell j}

\displaystyle M^{-1}.x_{i_{1}j_{1}}\dots x_{i_{r}j_{r}}

\displaystyle=\left(\sum_{\ell_{1}=1}^{n}m_{i_{1}\ell_{1}}x_{\ell_{1}j_{1}}\right)\cdots\left(\sum_{\ell_{r}=1}^{n}m_{i_{r}\ell_{r}}x_{\ell_{r}j_{r}}\right)

(1)

\displaystyle=\sum_{\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{r}=1}^{n}m_{i_{1}\ell_{1}}\cdots m_{i_{r}\ell_{r}}(x_{\ell_{1}j_{1}}\dots x_{\ell_{r}j_{r}})

In
[
OZ23
]
, the authors introduce a multiset partition algebra
{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(x)
with bases indexed by elements of
\tilde{\Pi}_{2(r),k}
. When
x
is specialized to an integer
n\geq 2r
, the algebra
{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n)
is isomorphic to
\End_{\mathfrak{S}_{n}}(\mathcal{P}^{r}(V_{n,k}))
where
\mathfrak{S}_{n}
acts by the restriction of the
GL_{n}
action above to the
n\times n
permutation matrices. The authors obtain a basis analogous to the orbit basis for
P_{r}(n)
and prove that for
n\geq 2r
the irreducible representations of
{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n)
occurring in the decomposition

(2)

\displaystyle\mathcal{P}^{r}(V_{n,k})\cong\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\Lambda^{{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n)}}W_{\mathfrak{S}_{n}}^{\lambda}\otimes W_{{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n)}^{\lambda}

have dimension
\dim(W_{{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n)}^{\lambda})=\#\mathcal{SSMPT}_{\lambda,r,k}
.

In
[
COS+20
]
, the authors generalize the Robinson–Schensted–Knuth algorithm to two-line arrays of multisets. This algorithm establishes a correspondence between multiset partitions in
\tilde{\Pi}_{2(r),k}
and pairs of elements of
\mathcal{SSMPT}_{\lambda,r,k}
,

\tilde{\Pi}_{2(r),k}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\longleftrightarrow}}\biguplus_{\lambda\in\Lambda^{{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n)}}\mathcal{SSMPT}_{\lambda,r,k}\times\mathcal{SSMPT}_{\lambda,r,k}

showing that

\displaystyle\dim({\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n))=\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\left(\dim(W_{{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n)}^{\lambda})\right)^{2}.

Hence, the
\left|\Lambda^{{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n)}\right|
irreducible representations occurring in Equation
2
are pairwise nonisomorphic, and each irreducible representation of
{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n)
is isomorphic to one representation in the set.

3.
Orbits Under Young Subgroups

The symmetric group algebra
\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{S}_{r}
sits naturally inside of
P_{r}(n)
as the diagrams whose blocks pair one vertex on top with one on the bottom. For
\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{r}
, we will write
\mathcal{L}_{\sigma}
for the diagram basis element corresponding to the set partition
\{\{\sigma(1),\bar{1}\},\dots\{\sigma(r),\bar{r}\}\}
. This embedding leads to natural actions on set partitions and set partition tableaux. In this section, we collect up some useful facts about orbits of these actions when they are restricted to Young subgroups. For
{\boldsymbol{a}}\in W_{r,k}
, write
\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{a}}=\mathfrak{S}_{\{1,\dots,{\boldsymbol{a}}_{1}\}}\times\dots\times\mathfrak{S}_{\{{\boldsymbol{a}}_{1}+\dots+{\boldsymbol{a}}_{k-1},\dots,{\boldsymbol{a}}_{1}+\dots+{\boldsymbol{a}}_{k}\}}
for the corresponding Young subgroup of
\mathfrak{S}_{r}
.

A pair of permutations
(\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2})\in\mathfrak{S}_{r}\times\mathfrak{S}_{r}
can act on a set partition
\pi\in\Pi_{2(r)}
by taking the product
\mathcal{L}_{\sigma_{1}}\mathcal{L}_{\pi}\mathcal{L}_{\sigma_{2}}
. The resulting set partition
\sigma_{1}.\pi.\sigma_{2}
can be obtained by replacing each
i
in
\pi
with
\sigma_{1}(i)
and each
\bar{i}
in
\pi
with
\bar{{\sigma_{2}}^{-1}(i)}
.

Given
{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}\in W_{r,k}
, define the
coloring map

\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}:\Pi_{2(r)}\to\tilde{\Pi}_{2(r)}
to be the function given by making the following substitutions.

\displaystyle i\mapsto\begin{cases}1&i\leq{\boldsymbol{a}}_{1}\\
2&{\boldsymbol{a}}_{1}<i\leq{\boldsymbol{a}}_{1}+{\boldsymbol{a}}_{2}\\
\vdots\\
k&{\boldsymbol{a}}_{1}+\dots+{\boldsymbol{a}}_{k-1}<i\end{cases}

\displaystyle\bar{i}\mapsto\begin{cases}\bar{1}&i\leq{\boldsymbol{b}}_{1}\\
\bar{2}&{\boldsymbol{b}}_{1}<i\leq{\boldsymbol{b}}_{1}+{\boldsymbol{b}}_{2}\\
\vdots\\
\bar{k}&{\boldsymbol{b}}_{1}+\dots+{\boldsymbol{b}}_{k-1}<i\end{cases}

On diagrams, we can think of
\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}
as coloring in the diagram of
\pi
with colors whose multiplicities are given by
{\boldsymbol{a}}
on top and
{\boldsymbol{b}}
on bottom.

Lemma 3.2
.

For
{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}\in W_{r,k}
, the map
\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}
induces a map

\displaystyle\bar{\kappa}_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}:\Pi_{2(r)}/(\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{a}}\times\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{b}})\rightarrow\tilde{\Pi}_{2(r),{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}

from set partitions modulo the action of
\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{a}}\times\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{b}}
to multiset partitions whose elements have multiplicities given by
{\boldsymbol{a}}
and
{\boldsymbol{b}}
. These maps taken together give a correspondence

(3)

\displaystyle\tilde{\Pi}_{2(r),k}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\longleftrightarrow}}\biguplus_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}\in W_{r,k}}\Pi_{2(r)}/(\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{a}}\times\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{b}})

Proof.

For
(\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2})\in\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{a}}\times\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{b}}
, it is clear that
\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}(\sigma_{1}.\pi.\sigma_{2})=\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}(\pi)
for all
\pi\in\Pi_{2(r)}
. Hence,
\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}
induces a map
\bar{\kappa}_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}:\Pi_{2(r)}/(\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{a}}\times\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{b}})\rightarrow\tilde{\Pi}_{2(r),k}
. Conversely, if
\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}(\pi)=\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}(\pi^{\prime})
, then
\pi
and
\pi^{\prime}
are in the same orbit. Hence, the map
\bar{\kappa}_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}
is injective. Given
{\tilde{\pi}}\in\tilde{\Pi}_{2(r),k}
whose unbarred and barred multiplicities are given by
{\boldsymbol{a}}
and
{\boldsymbol{b}}
respectively, we can easily create a set partition
\pi\in\Pi_{2(r)}
such that
\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}(\pi)={\tilde{\pi}}
by simply taking any graph representing
{\tilde{\pi}}
and forgetting the data of the colored vertices. Hence, the maps
\bar{\kappa}_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}
taken together as a map
\biguplus_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}\in W_{r,k}}\Pi_{2(r)}/(\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{a}}\times\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{b}})\to\tilde{\Pi}_{2(r),k}
give a bijection. This map gives us a correspondence between multiset partitions and orbits of set partitions under an action of a pair of Young subgroups.

∎

We now obtain a second action from the module structure of
P_{r}^{\lambda}
. A permutation
\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{r}
acts on the set
\mathcal{SPT}_{\lambda,r}
by replacing each entry
i
of a tableau
T
with
\sigma(i)
.

Lemma 3.5
.

There is a correspondence

\mathcal{MPT}_{\lambda,r,k}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\longleftrightarrow}}\biguplus_{{\boldsymbol{a}}\in W_{r,k}}\mathcal{SPT}_{\lambda,r}/\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{a}}

where the multiset partition tableau
\tilde{T}
maps to the set
\kappa_{\boldsymbol{a}}^{-1}(\tilde{T})
.

Proof.

The proof is completely analogous to that of Lemma
3.2

∎

Remark 3.6
.

The orbit of a standard set partition tableau
T
corresponds to a multiset partition tableau
{\tilde{T}}
whose rows and columns weakly increase. That is,
{\tilde{T}}
is semistandard except for possible repeats within columns.

4.
The Painted Algebra Construction

This section considers an algebra
B
with a subset
\{e_{1},\dots,e_{m}\}
of its idempotents (which we call
distinguished idempotents
) and
M
a
B
-module. We provide constructions of a new algebra
\tilde{B}
called the corresponding
painted algebra
and a
\tilde{B}
-module
\tilde{M}
called the
painted module
. First, we consider the setting in which this construction will naturally arise in Section
5
.

Lemma 4.1
.

Let
A
be an algebra and
V
a semisimple
A
-module. Let
e_{1},\dots,e_{m}\in\End_{A}(V)
be idempotents. Then

\displaystyle\End_{A}\left(\bigoplus_{i=1}^{m}e_{i}V\right)\cong\bigoplus_{i,j=1}^{m}e_{i}\End_{A}(V)e_{j}

where the product on the right hand side of
e_{i}\varphi e_{j}\in e_{i}\End_{A}(V)e_{j}
and
e_{k}\psi e_{\ell}\in e_{k}\End_{A}(V)e_{\ell}
is given by

\displaystyle(e_{i}\varphi e_{j})\cdot(e_{k}\psi e_{\ell})=\delta_{jk}e_{i}(\varphi e_{j}\psi)e_{\ell}\in e_{i}\End_{A}(V)e_{\ell}.

where the product to the right of the equal sign is taken in
\End_{A}(V)
and
\delta_{jk}
is the Kronecker delta function.

Proof.

First, note that

\displaystyle\End_{A}\left(\bigoplus_{i=1}^{m}e_{i}V\right)

\displaystyle\cong\bigoplus_{i,j=1}^{m}\Hom_{A}(e_{j}V,e_{i}V).

An element
e_{i}\varphi e_{j}\in e_{i}\End_{A}(V)e_{j}
can be viewed as a map
e_{j}V\to e_{i}V
, giving rise to an injective linear map
\Phi:e_{i}\End_{A}(V)e_{j}\to\Hom_{A}(e_{j}V,e_{i}V)
. Because
V
is semisimple, the submodule
e_{j}V
has a complementary submodule
U
so that
V=e_{j}V\oplus U
. A map
\psi:e_{j}V\to e_{i}V\subseteq V
can be extended to a map
\bar{\psi}:V\to V
by setting
\bar{\psi}(u)=0
for all
u\in U
. Then for any
e_{j}v\in e_{j}V
, we have that
e_{i}\bar{\psi}e_{j}(e_{j}v)=e_{i}\bar{\psi}(e_{j}v)=e_{i}\psi(e_{j}v)
. Hence, the map
\Phi
is also surjective, so it is an isomorphism.

\displaystyle\End_{A}\left(\bigoplus_{i=1}^{m}e_{i}V\right)

\displaystyle\cong\bigoplus_{i,j=1}^{m}e_{i}\End_{A}(V)e_{j}

Suppose
j\neq k
. The output of the map
e_{k}\psi e_{\ell}
is in
e_{k}V
, so the component of its output in
e_{j}V
is zero. Hence,
(e_{i}\varphi e_{j})\cdot(e_{k}\psi e_{\ell})=0
. If instead
j=k
, we have that
(e_{i}\varphi e_{j})\cdot(e_{k}\psi e_{\ell})=e_{i}\varphi e_{j}e_{k}\psi e_{\ell}
. Hence,

\displaystyle(e_{i}\varphi e_{j})\cdot(e_{k}\psi e_{\ell})

\displaystyle=\delta_{jk}e_{i}\varphi(e_{j})^{2}\psi e_{\ell}

\displaystyle=\delta_{jk}e_{i}(\varphi e_{j}\psi)e_{\ell}\in e_{i}\End_{A}(V)e_{\ell}

∎

Lemma
4.1
motivates the following definition.

Definition 4.2
.

For a semisimple algebra
B
along with distinguished idempotents
\{e_{1},\dots,e_{m}\}
, the corresponding painted algebra with respect to these idempotents is

{\tilde{B}}=\bigoplus_{i,j=1}^{m}e_{i}Be_{j}

with multiplication as in Lemma
4.1
. For a
B
-module
M
, the corresponding painted module with respect to these idempotents is

\tilde{M}=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{m}e_{i}M

where
(e_{i}be_{j}).e_{k}m=\delta_{jk}(e_{i}be_{j}).m
, the action on the right side of the equality begin that of
B
on
M
.

Example 4.3
.

We now illustrate the painted algebra construction with two extreme examples.

(a)

If
e_{1},\dots,e_{m}\in B
are already orthogonal idempotents which sum to the identity, then
\tilde{B}\cong B
, and the painted algebra simply corresponds to the usual decomposition of the algebra by a system of orthogonal idempotents.

(b)

If each of
e_{1},\dots,e_{m}\in B
are the identity, then

\tilde{B}\cong\underbrace{B\oplus\dots\oplus B}_{m}.

To conclude this section, we show that the irreducible
{\tilde{B}}
-modules are precisely the painted irreducible
B
-modules.

Lemma 4.4
.

Let
B
be a semisimple algebra along with distinguished idempotents
\{e_{1},\dots,e_{m}\}
. Then

(1)

For any simple
B
-module
S
, either
{\tilde{S}}=\{0\}
or
{\tilde{S}}
is a simple
{\tilde{B}}
-module.

(2)

For any simple
{\tilde{B}}
-module
P
, there is a simple
B
-module
S
so that
{\tilde{S}}\cong P
.

Proof.

a

(1)

Suppose
{\tilde{S}}\neq\{0\}
, let
\tilde{s}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}e_{i}s_{i}\in{\tilde{S}}
be nonzero, and fix any
j\in[m]
such that
e_{j}s_{j}
is nonzero. We show that any such
\tilde{s}
generates
{\tilde{S}}
as a
{\tilde{B}}
-module, and so
{\tilde{S}}
is simple. Note that
e_{j}\tilde{s}=e_{j}s_{j}\in e_{j}S\subseteq S
. Because
S
is simple, for any
e_{k}s\in S
there exists
b\in B
such that
be_{j}\tilde{s}=s
and so
e_{k}be_{j}\tilde{s}=e_{k}s
. Because the elements
e_{k}s
span
{\tilde{S}}
, we see that
{\tilde{S}}
is generated by any nonzero element and hence is simple.

(2)

The remainder of the proof generalizes an argument for the case of a single idempotent found in the proof of Theorem 1.10.14 of
[
Lin18
]
. Suppose
P
is a simple
{\tilde{B}}
-module and define a
B
-module

U=\left(\bigoplus_{i=1}^{m}Ae_{i}\right)\otimes_{{\tilde{B}}}P

where
B
acts on the direct sum by left-multiplication. Write
S=U/M
where
M
is a maximal submodule of
U
. Then
S
is a simple
B
-module. The goal is now to define a nonzero
{\tilde{B}}
-module map from
P
to the painted module
{\tilde{S}}
.

Consider the quotient map
q:U\to S
and suppose
e_{i}\otimes p\neq 0
. We claim that
e_{i}\otimes p
generates
U
as a
B
-module and hence
q(e_{i}\otimes p)\neq 0
(else
e_{i}\otimes t\in M
, which would mean that
M=U
). To show this, we need only demonstrate that for any fixed
\ell\in[m]
and
p^{\prime}\in P
, there exists an element
b\in B
such that
b.(e_{i}\otimes p)=e_{\ell}\otimes p^{\prime}
. Because
P
is a simple module and
e_{i}.p\neq 0
, there exists an element
\tilde{b}=\sum_{j,k}e_{j}b_{j,k}e_{k}\in{\tilde{B}}
such that

\displaystyle\tilde{b}.e_{i}\otimes p

\displaystyle=\sum_{j,k}e_{j}b_{j,k}e_{k}.e_{i}\otimes p

\displaystyle=(e_{1}+\dots+e_{m})\otimes(\sum_{j}e_{j}b_{j,i}e_{i}.p)

\displaystyle=(e_{1}+\dots+e_{m})\otimes e_{\ell}p^{\prime}

\displaystyle=e_{\ell}\otimes p^{\prime}.

Set
b=\sum_{j}e_{j}b_{j,i}e_{i}
. Then
b.e_{i}\otimes p=e_{\ell}\otimes p^{\prime}
.

Let
p\in P
be nonzero and note that in
{\tilde{B}}
we have
e_{1}+\dots+e_{m}=1
, so
(e_{1}+\dots+e_{m}).p=p
. Hence, some
e_{i}.p\neq 0
. Consider the map

e_{i}qe_{i}:e_{i}U\to e_{i}S.

Because
e_{i}.(e_{i}\otimes p)=e_{i}\otimes p\in e_{i}U
, we know that
e_{i}qe_{i}
is nonzero. Define a
{\tilde{B}}
-module map
\bigoplus_{i=1}^{m}e_{i}U\to\bigoplus_{i=1}^{m}e_{i}S
by
e_{j}r\mapsto e_{j}q(r)
. By the above observation, this is a nonzero module map. By Schur’s Lemma, it is an isomorphism and hence

\displaystyle{\tilde{S}}

\displaystyle\cong\bigoplus_{i=1}^{m}e_{i}U

\displaystyle\cong(\bigoplus_{i,j=1}^{m}e_{i}Be_{j})\otimes P

\displaystyle\cong P.

∎

5.
Painted Diagram Algebras and a Diagram-Like Basis

In this section, our goal is to decompose
\mathcal{P}^{r}(V_{n,k})
in a way that allows us to use the results of Section
4
.

Let
U_{\boldsymbol{a}}
be the span of monomials of the form
x_{i_{1}j_{1}}\cdots x_{i_{r}j_{r}}
where for each
1\leq m\leq k
, exactly
{\boldsymbol{a}}_{m}
of the values
j_{1},\dots,j_{r}
are equal to
m
. For example, the monomials
x_{11}x_{21}x_{23}
and
x_{21}x_{21}x_{23}
are both in
U_{(2,0,1)}\subset\mathcal{P}^{3}(V_{2,3})
. To apply Lemma
4.1
and Lemma
4.4
, we will need to write the subspace
U_{\boldsymbol{a}}
as the projection by some idempotent in
P_{r}(n)
. We define the following idempotent for
{\boldsymbol{a}}\in W_{r,k}
:

s_{\boldsymbol{a}}=\frac{1}{\left|\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{a}}\right|}\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{a}}}\mathcal{L}_{\sigma}.

From Equation
1
we see that the subspace
U_{\boldsymbol{a}}
is in fact a
GL_{n}
-submodule of
\mathcal{P}^{r}(V_{n,k})
. This gives a decomposition

\mathcal{P}^{r}(V_{n,k})=\bigoplus_{{\boldsymbol{a}}\in W_{r,k}}U_{\boldsymbol{a}}

as a
GL_{n}
-module. We now use this decomposition to construct a linear isomorphism
\Phi:\bigoplus_{{\boldsymbol{a}}\in W_{r,k}}s_{\boldsymbol{a}}{V_{n}}^{\otimes r}\to\mathcal{P}^{r}(V_{n,k})
.

For
{\boldsymbol{a}}\in W_{r,k}
, define a linear map
\Phi_{\boldsymbol{a}}:{V_{n}}^{\otimes r}\to U_{\boldsymbol{a}}
by

\Phi_{\boldsymbol{a}}(e_{i_{1}}\otimes\dots\otimes e_{i_{r}})=\prod_{m=1}^{{\boldsymbol{a}}_{1}}x_{i_{m}1}\prod_{m={\boldsymbol{a}}_{1}+1}^{{\boldsymbol{a}}_{1}+{\boldsymbol{a}}_{2}}x_{i_{m}2}\dots\prod_{m={\boldsymbol{a}}_{1}+\dots+{\boldsymbol{a}}_{k-1}+1}^{r}x_{i_{m}k}.

Example 5.1
.

Note that two different tensors may map to equal monomials as in the following example.

\displaystyle\Phi_{(1,2,2)}(e_{2}\otimes e_{2}\otimes e_{1}\otimes e_{1}\otimes e_{2})

\displaystyle=x_{21}x_{22}x_{12}x_{13}x_{23}

\displaystyle\Phi_{(1,2,2)}(e_{2}\otimes e_{1}\otimes e_{2}\otimes e_{1}\otimes e_{2})

\displaystyle=x_{21}x_{12}x_{22}x_{13}x_{23}

Here, the tensors map to the same monomial because the second is obtained from the first by swapping two factors mapping to indeterminates of the same form
x_{i2}
.

For ease of notation, we will write
e_{\boldsymbol{i}}=e_{{\boldsymbol{i}}_{1}}\otimes\dots\otimes e_{{\boldsymbol{i}}_{r}}
for
{\boldsymbol{i}}\in[n]^{r}
. It is clear that
\Phi_{\boldsymbol{a}}
is surjective and that
\Phi_{\boldsymbol{a}}(e_{\boldsymbol{i}})=\Phi_{\boldsymbol{a}}(e_{{\boldsymbol{i}}^{\prime}})
exactly when
e_{{\boldsymbol{i}}^{\prime}}
can be obtained from
e_{\boldsymbol{i}}
by rearranging factors grouped into the same product above. That is,
e_{{\boldsymbol{i}}^{\prime}}=\sigma(e_{\boldsymbol{i}})
for some
\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{a}}
. Hence,
\Phi_{\boldsymbol{a}}
restricts to an isomorphism
s_{\boldsymbol{a}}{V_{n}}^{\otimes r}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\longrightarrow}}U_{\boldsymbol{a}}
, so the map
\Phi:\bigoplus_{{\boldsymbol{a}}\in W_{r,k}}s_{\boldsymbol{a}}{V_{n}}^{\otimes r}\to\mathcal{P}^{r}(V_{n,k})
sending
s_{\boldsymbol{a}}(e_{\boldsymbol{i}})
to
\Phi_{\boldsymbol{a}}(s_{\boldsymbol{a}}(e_{\boldsymbol{i}}))
is an isomorphism.

Lemma 5.2
.

The linear isomorphism
\Phi:\bigoplus_{{\boldsymbol{a}}\in W_{r,k}}s_{\boldsymbol{a}}{V_{n}}^{\otimes r}\to\mathcal{P}^{r}(V_{n,k})
above induces an isomorphism of algebras

\End_{G}(\mathcal{P}^{r}(V_{n,k}))\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\longrightarrow}}\End_{G}\left(\bigoplus_{{\boldsymbol{a}}\in W_{r,k}}s_{\boldsymbol{a}}{V_{n}}^{\otimes r}\right)

for each subgroup
G
of
GL_{n}
.

Proof.

The action of
M\in GL_{n}
on
s_{\boldsymbol{a}}(e_{i_{1}}\otimes\dots\otimes e_{i_{r}})
is given by

\displaystyle M.s_{\boldsymbol{a}}(e_{i_{1}}\otimes\dots\otimes e_{i_{r}})

\displaystyle=s_{\boldsymbol{a}}(Me_{i_{1}}\otimes\dots\otimes Me_{i_{r}})

\displaystyle=\sum_{\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{r}=1}^{n}m_{i_{1}\ell_{r}}\cdots m_{i_{r}\ell_{r}}s_{\boldsymbol{a}}(e_{\ell_{1}}\otimes\dots\otimes e_{\ell_{r}}).

Comparing this computation with Equation
1
, we see that the map
\Phi
is
nearly
a homomorphism of
GL_{n}
-modules, but the action of
M\in GL_{n}
on one space is the action of
M^{-1}
on the other. That is, for
M\in GL_{n}
,

\displaystyle\Phi M

\displaystyle=M^{-1}\Phi.

Multiplying by
\Phi^{-1}
on the left and right of both sides yields an analogous statement for
\Phi^{-1}
:

\displaystyle M\Phi^{-1}

\displaystyle=\Phi^{-1}M^{-1}.

The linear isomorphism
\Phi
induces an algebra isomorphism

\displaystyle\End_{\mathbb{C}}(\mathcal{P}^{r}(V_{n,k}))

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\longrightarrow}}\End_{\mathbb{C}}\left(\bigoplus_{{\boldsymbol{a}}\in W_{r,k}}s_{\boldsymbol{a}}{V_{n}}^{\otimes r}\right)

\displaystyle\varphi

\displaystyle\longmapsto\Phi^{-1}\varphi\Phi.

Now we make the following observation for
G\subseteq GL_{n}
a subgroup.

\displaystyle\varphi\in\End_{G}(\mathcal{P}^{r}(V_{n,k}))

\displaystyle\iff\varphi=M^{-1}\varphi M

\displaystyle\forall M\in G

\displaystyle\iff\Phi^{-1}\varphi\Phi=\Phi^{-1}M^{-1}\varphi M\Phi

\displaystyle\forall M\in G

\displaystyle\iff\Phi^{-1}\varphi\Phi=M\Phi^{-1}\varphi\Phi M^{-1}

\displaystyle\forall M\in G

\displaystyle\iff\Phi^{-1}\varphi\Phi\in\End_{G}\left(\bigoplus_{{\boldsymbol{a}}\in W_{r,k}}s_{\boldsymbol{a}}{V_{n}}^{\otimes r}\right)

Hence, the map
\varphi\mapsto\Phi^{-1}\varphi\Phi
restricts to an isomorphism

\End_{G}(\mathcal{P}^{r}{V_{n,k}}^{\otimes r})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\longrightarrow}}\End_{G}\left(\bigoplus_{{\boldsymbol{a}}\in W_{r,k}}s_{\boldsymbol{a}}{V_{n}}^{\otimes r}\right).

∎

Let
G
be a subgroup of
GL_{n}
. Because
G\subseteq GL_{n}
, we have that

\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{S}_{n}\cong\End_{GL_{n}}({V_{n}}^{\otimes r})\subseteq\End_{G}({V_{n}}^{\otimes r}).

Hence, the idempotents
s_{\boldsymbol{a}}
for
{\boldsymbol{a}}\in W_{r,k}
are in
\End_{G}({V_{n}}^{\otimes r})
, allowing us to use Lemma
4.1
to make the following computation.

\displaystyle\End_{G}\left(\mathcal{P}^{r}(V_{n,k})\right)

\displaystyle\cong\End_{G}\left(\bigoplus_{{\boldsymbol{a}}\in W_{r,k}}s_{\boldsymbol{a}}{V_{n}}^{\otimes r}\right)

\displaystyle\cong\bigoplus_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}\in W_{r,k}}s_{\boldsymbol{a}}\End_{G}({V_{n}}^{\otimes r})s_{\boldsymbol{b}}

where the product is given by

(4)

\displaystyle(s_{\boldsymbol{a}}\varphi s_{\boldsymbol{b}})\cdot(s_{\boldsymbol{c}}\psi s_{\boldsymbol{d}})=\delta_{{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}s_{\boldsymbol{a}}\varphi s_{\boldsymbol{b}}\psi s_{\boldsymbol{d}}.

If we write
A_{r}(n)=\End_{G}({V_{n}}^{\otimes r})
, this algebra is precisely the painted algebra
\tilde{A}_{r,k}(n)
with respect to the idempotents
\{s_{\boldsymbol{a}}:{\boldsymbol{a}}\in W_{r,k}\}
. We summarize the above analysis in the following theorem.

Theorem 5.3
.

Let
G\subseteq GL_{n}
be a subgroup and let
A_{r}(n)=\End_{G}\left({V_{n}}^{\otimes r}\right)
. Then

\End_{G}\left(\mathcal{P}^{r}(V_{n,k})\right)\cong\tilde{A}_{r,k}(n)

where
\tilde{A}_{r,k}(n)
is the painted algebra of
A_{r}(n)
with respect to the idempotents
\{s_{\boldsymbol{a}}:{\boldsymbol{a}}\in W_{r,k}\}
.

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{r}(n)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces GL_{n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\tilde{A}_{r,k}(n)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{V_{n}}^{\otimes r}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{P}^{r}(V_{n,k})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathfrak{S}_{r}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces GL_{k}}

Figure 1.
This diagram illustrates how Theorem
5.3
relates the centralizers of a group
G
under Schur-Weyl duality (left) and Howe duality (right). Note that the diagonals should only be taken to signify
mutual
centralizers when the conditions of the double-centralizer theorem are satisfied (e.g. when
G
is a linear reductive subgroup).

Now, we use this isomorphism to construct a basis for
{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n)\cong\End_{\mathfrak{S}_{n}}(\mathcal{P}^{r}(V_{n,k}))
from the diagram basis of
P_{r}(n)
. Such a basis can be similarly constructed for other subalgebras of
P_{r}(n)
that contain
\mathfrak{S}_{r}
(see Remark
5.7
). In general, the projection
s_{\boldsymbol{a}}L_{\pi}s_{\boldsymbol{b}}
can be computed as follows.

\displaystyle s_{\boldsymbol{a}}\mathcal{L}_{\pi}s_{\boldsymbol{b}}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\left|\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{a}}\times\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{b}}\right|}\sum_{(\sigma,\sigma^{\prime})\in\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{a}}\times\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{b}}}\mathcal{L}_{\sigma}\mathcal{L}_{\pi}\mathcal{L}_{\sigma^{\prime}}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\left|\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{a}}\times\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{b}}\right|}\sum_{(\sigma,\sigma^{\prime})\in\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{a}}\times\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{b}}}\mathcal{L}_{\sigma.\pi.\sigma^{\prime}}

Each diagram basis element
\mathcal{L}_{\pi}
projects to the sum of the orbit of
\pi
under the
\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{a}}\times\mathfrak{S}_{{\boldsymbol{b}}}
-action. Because the orbits are disjoint, the set of distinct projections are linearly independent and hence form a basis of
s_{\boldsymbol{a}}P_{r}(n)s_{\boldsymbol{b}}
. Due to the correspondence between orbits of set partitions under the action of a Young subgroup and multiset partitions given in Section
3
, we know that these basis elements are indexed by multiset partitions obtained by applying the map
\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}
to set partitions. Diagrammatically, this corresponds to coloring in the vertices of elements in
\Pi_{2(r)}
with colors whose multiplicities are given by
{\boldsymbol{a}}
on the top and
{\boldsymbol{b}}
on the bottom.

For
{\tilde{\pi}}\in\tilde{\Pi}_{2(r),k}
define
\mathcal{D}_{\tilde{\pi}}=s_{\boldsymbol{a}}\mathcal{L}_{\pi}s_{\boldsymbol{b}}
where
\pi
is any set partition in the orbit corresponding to
{\tilde{\pi}}
. We then see that
\{\mathcal{D}_{\tilde{\pi}}:{\tilde{\pi}}\in\tilde{\Pi}\}
is a basis for
\tilde{P}_{r,k}(n)\cong{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n)
. Using the formula in Lemma
4.1
, the product
\mathcal{D}_{\tilde{\pi}}\mathcal{D}_{\tilde{\nu}}
for
{\tilde{\pi}}\in\tilde{\Pi}_{2(r),k}
with multiplicities on top and bottom given by
{\boldsymbol{a}}
and
{\boldsymbol{b}}
respectively and
{\tilde{\nu}}\in\tilde{\Pi}_{2(r),k}
with multiplicities on top and bottom given by
{\boldsymbol{b}}^{\prime}
and
{\boldsymbol{c}}
respectively is the following.

\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{\tilde{\pi}}\mathcal{D}_{\tilde{\nu}}

\displaystyle=(s_{\boldsymbol{a}}\mathcal{L}_{\pi}s_{\boldsymbol{b}})\cdot(s_{{\boldsymbol{b}}^{\prime}}\mathcal{L}_{\nu}s_{\boldsymbol{c}})

\displaystyle=\delta_{{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{b}}^{\prime}}s_{\boldsymbol{a}}\mathcal{L}_{\pi}s_{\boldsymbol{b}}\mathcal{L}_{\nu}s_{\boldsymbol{c}}

\displaystyle=\frac{\delta_{{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{b}}^{\prime}}}{\left|\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{b}}\right|}\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{b}}}s_{\boldsymbol{a}}\mathcal{L}_{\pi}\mathcal{L}_{\sigma}\mathcal{L}_{\nu}s_{\boldsymbol{c}}

\displaystyle=\frac{\delta_{{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{b}}^{\prime}}}{\left|\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{b}}\right|}\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{b}}}s_{\boldsymbol{a}}\mathcal{L}_{\pi}\mathcal{L}_{\sigma.\nu}s_{\boldsymbol{c}}

To interpret this product combinatorially, it will be helpful to assign a combinatorial object to each term in the sum.

Definition 5.4
.

For a pair
{\tilde{\pi}},{\tilde{\nu}}\in\tilde{\Pi}_{2(r),k}
, a
snapshot
is a pair
(\pi,\nu)
where
\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}(\pi)={\tilde{\pi}}
and
\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}={\tilde{\nu}}
. We can represent these visually as a stack of partition diagrams whose vertices are painted from
k
colors. To differentiate from the multiset partition diagrams (and to emphasize that the identically colored vertices in this situation are not interchangeable and are instead fixed in place), we draw the vertices as open circles.

The formula above can then be thought of as beginning with any snapshot
(\pi,\nu)
and them summing over the snapshots
\{(\pi,\sigma.\nu):\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{b}}\}
. In the summand,
\mathcal{L}_{\pi}\mathcal{L}_{\sigma.\nu}
is the product of the two set partitions as elements of
P_{r}(n)
and multiplying by the idempotents
s_{\boldsymbol{a}}
and
s_{\boldsymbol{b}}
projects to the diagram-like basis element corresponding to the multiset partition obtained by filling in the vertices.

because if the vertices were filled in, the resulting multiset partition diagrams would still be identical to the two we are taking the product of.

We call this basis
\{D_{\tilde{\pi}}:{\tilde{\pi}}\in\tilde{\Pi}_{2r,k}\}
for
{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n)\cong\End_{\mathfrak{S}_{n}}(\mathcal{P}^{r}(V_{n,k}))
the
diagram-like basis
.

Remark 5.6
.

This perspective resolves the question of how the multiset partition algebra
{\rm M\!P\!}_{\boldsymbol{a}}(n)
for
{\boldsymbol{a}}\in W_{r,k}
defined in
[
NPS23
]
sits inside
{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n)
:

\displaystyle{\rm M\!P\!}_{{\boldsymbol{a}}}(n)

\displaystyle\cong\End_{\mathfrak{S}_{n}}(s_{\boldsymbol{a}}{V_{n}}^{\otimes r})

\displaystyle\cong s_{\boldsymbol{a}}P_{r}(n)s_{\boldsymbol{a}}.

Note that
s_{\boldsymbol{a}}P_{r}(n)s_{\boldsymbol{a}}
is the span of diagram-like basis elements in
{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n)
whose colors on top and bottom have multiplicity given by
{\boldsymbol{a}}
.

Remark 5.7
.

Let
A_{r}(n)\subseteq P_{r}(n)
be a subalgebra spanned by the diagram-basis elements indexed by the set partitions in some set
\Pi
. If
\Pi
contains the set partitions corresponding to the symmetric group
\mathfrak{S}_{r}
, then the construction of the diagram-like basis above restricts to the painted version of this subalgebra. In particular,
\tilde{A}_{r,k}(n)
has basis given by the diagram-like basis elements indexed by
\biguplus_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}\in W_{r,k}}\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}(\Pi)
.

For a concrete example, the Brauer algebra
B_{r}(n)
is the subalgebra of
P_{r}(n)
spanned by the set partition diagrams whose blocks are all of size two. The corresponding painted Brauer algebra
\tilde{B}_{r,k}(n)
has a basis indexed by the multiset partition diagrams whose blocks are all of size two.

Note that planar subalgebras of
P_{r}(n)
(such as the Temperley-Lieb algebra) do not contain the symmetric group, and hence this painted algebra construction does not extend nicely to them. It may be the case that there are painted analogues of these planar algebras which centralize a group action on
\mathcal{P}^{r}(V_{n,k})
, but they do not seem amenable to description with the methods of this paper.

6.
Irreducible Representations of
{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n)

In this section, we aim to construct the irreducible representations of
{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n)
. Part (2) of Lemma
4.4
tells us that in order to construct each of these irreducible representations, we need only consider the irreducible
P_{r}(n)
representations painted with respect to the idempotents
\{s_{\boldsymbol{a}}:{\boldsymbol{a}}\in W_{r,k}\}
. For
\lambda\in\Lambda^{P_{r}(n)}
, define

{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}^{\lambda}\vcentcolon=\tilde{P_{r}^{\lambda}}=\bigoplus_{{\boldsymbol{a}}\in W_{r,k}}s_{\boldsymbol{a}}P_{r}^{\lambda}.

By Lemma
4.4
, each module in
\{{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}^{\lambda}:\lambda\in\Lambda^{P_{r}(n)}\}
is either a simple
{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n)
-module or the zero module, and each simple
{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n)
module appears in the set. To investigate the structure of these modules, we note that for
T\in\mathcal{SPT}_{\lambda,r}
, the projection
s_{\boldsymbol{a}}v_{T}
is the average over the
\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{a}}
-orbit of
T
:

s_{\boldsymbol{a}}v_{T}=\frac{1}{\left|\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{a}}.T\right|}\sum_{S\in\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{a}}.T}v_{S}

This orbit corresponds to
{\tilde{T}}=\kappa_{\boldsymbol{a}}(T)\in\mathcal{MPT}_{\lambda,r,k}
, and so we define

w_{\tilde{T}}=s_{\boldsymbol{a}}v_{T}=\frac{1}{\left|\kappa_{\boldsymbol{a}}^{-1}({\tilde{T}})\right|}\sum_{T\in\kappa_{\boldsymbol{a}}^{-1}({\tilde{T}})}v_{T}

where
\kappa_{\boldsymbol{a}}^{-1}({\tilde{T}})
is the preimage of
{\tilde{T}}
under the coloring map.

Lemma 6.1
.

If
T\in\mathcal{SSPT}_{\lambda,r}
, then either
w_{\tilde{T}}=0
or
{\tilde{T}}\in\mathcal{SSMPT}_{\lambda,r,k}
.

Proof.

As observed in Remark
3.6
, if
T\in\mathcal{SSPT}_{\lambda,r}
, then
{\tilde{T}}
has rows and columns weakly increasing. If
{\tilde{T}}
is not semistandard, then it must have two boxes within the same column that have identical contents. For a tableau
T
, write
T^{\prime}
for the tableau obtained by swapping the content of these two boxes. Then

w_{{\tilde{T}}}=w_{\tilde{T^{\prime}}}=\frac{1}{\left|\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{a}}.T\right|}\sum_{S\in\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{a}}.T}v_{S^{\prime}}=\frac{1}{\left|\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{a}}.T\right|}\sum_{S\in\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{a}}.T}-v_{S}=-w_{{\tilde{T}}}.

Hence, if
{\tilde{T}}\notin\mathcal{SSMPT}_{\lambda,r,k}
, then
w_{\tilde{T}}=0
.
∎

We can now use Lemma
6.1
to describe a straightening algorithm for
{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}^{\lambda}
. Suppose
{\tilde{T}}
is not semistandard and
w_{\tilde{T}}\neq 0
. Then there exists a nonstandard
T
in the
\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{a}}
-orbit corresponding to
{\tilde{T}}
. Then using the straightening algorithm for
P_{r}^{\lambda}
, we can write

v_{T}=\sum_{S\in\mathcal{SSPT}_{\lambda,r}}c_{S}v_{S}.

Then projecting by
s_{\boldsymbol{a}}
, we obtain

w_{\tilde{T}}=s_{\boldsymbol{a}}v_{T}=\sum_{S\in\mathcal{SSPT}_{\lambda,r}}c_{S}s_{\boldsymbol{a}}v_{S}=\sum_{S\in\mathcal{SSPT}_{\lambda,r}}c_{S}w_{\tilde{S}}

where each
{\tilde{S}}
for which
w_{{\tilde{S}}}\neq 0
is semistandard.

Theorem 6.2
.

The set
\{{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}^{\lambda}:\lambda\in\Lambda^{{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n)}\}
forms a complete set of irreducible representations for
{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n)
and for each
\lambda\in\Lambda^{{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n)}
, the set
\{w_{\tilde{T}}:{\tilde{T}}\in\mathcal{SSMPT}_{\lambda,r,k}\}
forms a basis of
{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}^{\lambda}
.

Proof.

Because
{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}^{\lambda}
is the span of
\{w_{\tilde{T}}:{\tilde{T}}\in\mathcal{SSMPT}_{\lambda,r,k}\}
, we know that
{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}^{\lambda}=0
unless
\lambda\in\Lambda^{{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n)}
. We then have that each of the
\left|\Lambda^{{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n)}\right|
irreducible representations appears in the smaller set
\{{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}^{\lambda}:\lambda\in\Lambda^{{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n)}\}
. Because there are only
\left|\Lambda^{{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n)}\right|
representations in this set, it must be a complete set of irreducible representations for
{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n)
.

A priori, we do not know that these
w_{\tilde{T}}
are linearly independent, so we can only conclude that
\dim({\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}^{\lambda})\leq\#\mathcal{SSMPT}_{\lambda,r,k}
. However, we do know that

\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda^{{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n)}}(\dim({\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}^{\lambda}))^{2}=\dim({\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n))=\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda^{{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n)}}(\#\mathcal{SSMPT}_{\lambda,r,k})^{2}.

Hence
\dim({\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}^{\lambda})=\#\mathcal{SSMPT}_{\lambda,r,k}
and so for each
\lambda\in\Lambda^{{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n)}
the set
\{w_{\tilde{T}}:{\tilde{T}}\in\mathcal{SSMPT}_{\lambda,r,k}\}
indeed forms a basis of
{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}^{\lambda}
.
∎

We now consider the action of an element
\mathcal{D}_{\tilde{\pi}}
on
w_{\tilde{T}}
. Suppose that the multiplicities of colors in
{\tilde{\pi}}
are given by
{\boldsymbol{a}}
and
{\boldsymbol{b}}
respectively and that the multiplicities of elements in
{\tilde{T}}
are given by
{\boldsymbol{c}}
. Then the definition of a painted module gives us the following formula:

\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{\tilde{\pi}}.w_{\tilde{T}}

\displaystyle=s_{\boldsymbol{a}}L_{\pi}s_{\boldsymbol{b}}.s_{\boldsymbol{c}}v_{T}

\displaystyle=\delta_{{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(s_{\boldsymbol{a}}L_{\pi}s_{\boldsymbol{b}}v_{T})

\displaystyle=\delta_{{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{b}}}s_{\boldsymbol{a}}L_{\pi.\sigma}v_{T}

We can interpret this formula for diagrams as follows.

(i)

Pull out the content of
{\tilde{T}}
, a multiset partition with
r
elements from
[k]
, in a row above and fix the order.

(ii)

Place
{\tilde{\pi}}
on top and permute the vertices of the same color at the bottom in each possible way.

(iii)

For each permutation, compute the action as for
P_{r}^{\lambda}
.

(iv)

Sum the resulting tableaux and divide by the number of permutations.

Example 6.3
.

The action of a multiset partition on a multiset partition tableau. Note that in the latter two permutations of the diagram, the content of the box in the second row does not reach the top of the diagram, so the output is zero.

7.
Generators

To describe a generating set for
{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n)
, we will give an algorithm for factoring out certain blocks from a diagram.

Definition 7.1
.

We call a block of the form
\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{i,\bar{i}\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}
a
vertical bar
. A block of a multiset partition
{\tilde{\pi}}
that is not a vertical bar or a singleton is called a
nonbasic block
. For a set partition
\pi
with
\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}(\pi)={\tilde{\pi}}
, we call a vertex in the diagram of
\pi

nonbasic
if it is mapped to a nonbasic block under
\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}
.

We now define a statistic on multiset partitions and prove a lemma about how this statistic interacts with the diagram-like product.

Definition 7.2
.

Write
N({\tilde{\pi}})
for the multiset of nonbasic blocks of
{\tilde{\pi}}
and define the
nonbasic weight
of
{\tilde{\pi}}
to be

\nbw({\tilde{\pi}})=\sum_{{\tilde{B}}\in N({\tilde{\pi}})}\left|{\tilde{B}}\right|.

.

\displaystyle=2+3+4=9

Lemma 7.4
.

If
\mathcal{D}_{\tilde{\nu}}
appears with nonzero coefficient in the product
\mathcal{D}_{{\tilde{\pi}}_{1}}\mathcal{D}_{{\tilde{\pi}}_{2}}
, then

\nbw({\tilde{\nu}})\leq\nbw({\tilde{\pi}}_{1})+\nbw({\tilde{\pi}}_{2})

with equality if and only if
N({\tilde{\nu}})=N({\tilde{\pi}}_{1})\uplus N({\tilde{\pi}}_{2})
.

Proof.

Consider a snapshot
(\pi_{1},\pi_{2})
in the product
\mathcal{D}_{{\tilde{\pi}}_{1}}\mathcal{D}_{{\tilde{\pi}}_{2}}
and suppose
\mathcal{L}_{\pi_{1}}\mathcal{L}_{\pi_{2}}=n^{c}\mathcal{L}_{\nu}
. Suppose
{\tilde{\pi}}_{1}=\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}(\pi_{1})
and
{\tilde{\pi}}_{2}=\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\pi_{2})
. Write
{\tilde{\nu}}=\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\nu)
. Our goal is now to construct an injective map
\varphi
from the set of nonbasic vertices of
\nu
to the nonbasic vertices of
\pi_{1}
and
\pi_{2}
.

Consider a nonbasic vertex
v
of
\nu
labeled
i
. There is a corresponding vertex
v^{\prime}
of
\pi_{1}
also labeled
i
. If
v^{\prime}
is the only element in its block, the same is true for
v
. Hence,
v^{\prime}
must either be a nonbasic vertex or one end of a vertical bar. In the first case, set
\varphi(v)
equal to
v^{\prime}
, which is nonbasic. In the latter case, let
\bar{j}
be the label of the other vertex in the vertical bar and let
\varphi(v)
be the vertex of
\pi_{2}
labeled
j
. If the diagram of
\pi_{1}
were set atop that of
\pi_{2}
, this would be the vertex on the top of
\pi_{2}
that the vertical bar lands on. If
v
is labeled
\bar{i}
, the same process is followed swapping which elements are barred (see Figure
2
for an illustration of this map).

Figure 2.
Illustration of the injective map
\varphi
constructed in Lemma
7.4
. The nonbasic vertices on the right and the corresponding nonbasic vertices in the image of
\varphi
on the left are highlighted in green.

In the latter case, if
\varphi(v)
is basic, it is either the only element of its block (in which case,
v
would be a singleton) or part of a vertical bar (in which case,
v
is in a vertical bar). Either way, this contradicts the assumption that
\nu
is nonbasic, so we have constructed a map
\varphi
from the set of nonbasic vertices of
\nu
to the nonbasic vertices of
\pi_{1}
and
\pi_{2}
. It is clear that this map is injective, and so the number of nonbasic vertices of
\nu
is less than the total number of nonbasic vertices of

\pi_{1}
and
\pi_{2}
, giving us the desired inequality.

Now to investigate the case of equality we consider how the map
\varphi
interacts with the set partition structure. Suppose that
\varphi(v)
and
\varphi(w)
are in the same block. Without loss of generality, assume they are in the same block of
\pi_{1}
. We then need to consider the following cases: (see Figure
3
(i)-(iii) for illustrations of these cases)

(i)

\varphi(v)
and
\varphi(w)
are both on the top of the block.

The vertex
\varphi(v)
has the same label as
v
and
\varphi(w)
has the same label as
w
. Because the vertices with these labels are connected, the vertices with the same labels must be connected in the product, so
v
and
w
are in the same block.

(ii)

\varphi(v)
and
\varphi(w)
are both on the bottom of the block.

The vertices
\varphi(v)
and
\varphi(w)
each meet a vertical bar whose other end is labeled the same as
v
and
w
respectively. Hence,
v
and
w
are joined in the product.

(iii)

Without loss of generality
\varphi(v)
is on the top of the block and
\varphi(w)
is on the bottom.

The vertex
\varphi(v)
is labeled the same as
v
and the vertex on the other end of the vertical bar meeting
\varphi(w)
is labeled the same as
w
. Hence
v
and
w
are again joined in the product.

Hence, if
\varphi(v)
and
\varphi(w)
are in the same block, then
u
and
v
are in the same block.

Suppose that
v
and
w
are in the same block but
\varphi(v)
and
\varphi(w)
are not (see Figure
3
(iv)-(v)). Then two nonbasic blocks in the product must have been combined, and any vertex where the two nonbasic blocks meet must not be in the image of
\varphi
, meaning
\varphi
is not a surjection in this case.

When equality holds, the map
\varphi
is a bijection and
\varphi(v)
in the same block as
\varphi(w)
if and only if
v
and
w
are in the same block. The map
\varphi
then induces a bijection of nonbasic
blocks
, hence
N({\tilde{\nu}})=N({\tilde{\pi}}_{1})\uplus N({\tilde{\pi}}_{2})
.
∎

Figure 3.
Illustrations of cases when
\varphi(u)
and
\varphi(w)
are in the same block.

We will introduce a sort of factorization of a diagram
{\tilde{\pi}}
with a nonbasic block
{\tilde{B}}
into diagrams with fewer nonbasic blocks, and to that end we define two diagrams
{\tilde{\pi}}/{\tilde{B}}
and
{\tilde{\pi}}|_{{\tilde{B}}}
. Informally, the diagram
{\tilde{\pi}}/{\tilde{B}}
is the result of removing the block
{\tilde{B}}
and replacing it with basic blocks, and the diagram
{\tilde{\pi}}|_{{\tilde{B}}}
is a diagram whose only nonbasic block is
{\tilde{B}}
.

Example 7.5
.

Here we show how the diagram
{\tilde{\pi}}
can be factored at the nonbasic block
{\tilde{B}}
.

Note that in
{\tilde{\pi}}|_{{\tilde{B}}}
, the block
{\tilde{B}}
is joined by vertical bars matching the remaining vertices atop
{\tilde{\pi}}
as well as two singletons
\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{\bar{1}\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}
at the bottom so that the number of vertices on top and on bottom match. In
{\tilde{\pi}}/{\tilde{B}}
, the block
{\tilde{B}}
is removed from
{\tilde{\pi}}
, leaving behind a vertical bar matching each vertex at the bottom of
{\tilde{B}}
as well as two singletons
\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{1\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}
so that the number of vertices on top and on bottom again match.

We now define this factorization more precisely.

Definition 7.6
.

Let
{\tilde{\pi}}\in\tilde{\Pi}_{2r,k}
have a nonbasic block
{\tilde{B}}
. Without loss of generality, assume
{\tilde{B}}
has more unbarred entries than barred entries. Write
{\tilde{\pi}}/{\tilde{B}}
for the multiset partition obtained by replacing
{\tilde{B}}
with vertical bars
\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{i,\bar{i}\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}
for each barred entry
\bar{i}
of
{\tilde{B}}
and a number of singletons
\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{\bar{1}\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}
making up the difference in the number of barred and unbarred entries in
{\tilde{B}}
. Write
{\tilde{\pi}}|_{{\tilde{B}}}
for the multiset partition consisting of
{\tilde{B}}
, a vertical bar
\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{i,\bar{i}\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}
for each vertex labeled
i
in
{\tilde{\pi}}
not in
{\tilde{B}}
, and enough
\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{\bar{1}\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}
to make it an element of
\tilde{\Pi}_{2(r),k}
.

We see immediately in Example
7.5
that although the element
\mathcal{D}_{\tilde{\pi}}
will appear with nonzero coefficient in
\mathcal{D}_{{\tilde{\pi}}|_{{\tilde{B}}}}\mathcal{D}_{{\tilde{\pi}}/{\tilde{B}}}
, many diagrams other than
\mathcal{D}_{\tilde{\pi}}
also appear. To systematically account for these extra diagrams, we now define a partial order in which they are smaller than the desired diagram
\mathcal{D}_{\tilde{\pi}}
. This will allow us to use the factorization recursively to write
\mathcal{D}_{\tilde{\pi}}
as a polynomial in simpler diagrams.

Write
\vb({\tilde{\pi}})
for the number of vertical bars in
{\tilde{\pi}}
. Define a partial order on
\tilde{\Pi}_{r,k}
by saying that
{\tilde{\pi}}\prec{\tilde{\tau}}
if either

\displaystyle\nbw({\tilde{\pi}})

\displaystyle<\nbw({\tilde{\tau}})

or

\displaystyle\nbw({\tilde{\pi}})=\nbw({\tilde{\tau}})

\displaystyle\text{ and }\vb({\tilde{\pi}})<\vb({\tilde{\tau}}).

Lemma 7.7
.

Let
{\tilde{\pi}}
be a multiset partition and
{\tilde{B}}
a nonbasic block of
{\tilde{\pi}}
with more unbarred entries than barred entries. Then there is a constant
c\in\mathbb{C}
so that

c\mathcal{D}_{{\tilde{\pi}}|_{{\tilde{B}}}}\mathcal{D}_{{\tilde{\pi}}/{\tilde{B}}}-\mathcal{D}_{\tilde{\pi}}\in\Span_{\mathbb{C}}\{\mathcal{D}_{\tilde{\nu}}:{\tilde{\nu}}\prec{\tilde{\pi}}\}.

Proof.

Consider a snapshot in the product
\mathcal{D}_{{\tilde{\pi}}|_{{\tilde{B}}}}\mathcal{D}_{{\tilde{\pi}}/{\tilde{B}}}
in which each vertex at the bottom of the block
{\tilde{B}}
in
{\tilde{\pi}}|_{{\tilde{B}}}
meets a vertical bar in
{\tilde{\pi}}/{\tilde{B}}
and each singleton
\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{\bar{1}\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}
in
{\tilde{\pi}}|_{{\tilde{B}}}
created in the factorization meets a singleton
\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{1\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}
in
{\tilde{\pi}}/{\tilde{B}}
created during the factorization. Such a snapshot exists because there is a vertical bar in
{\tilde{\pi}}|_{{\tilde{B}}}
matching each vertex at the bottom of
{\tilde{B}}
and the number of singletons added to each factor is precisely the difference between the number of vertices in the top and in the bottom of
{\tilde{B}}
. The resulting diagram from this snapshot is
{\tilde{\pi}}
, and so
\mathcal{D}_{\tilde{\pi}}
appears with nonzero coefficient in the product. Let
c
be the reciprocal of the coefficient it appears with.

By Lemma
7.4
any
\mathcal{D}_{\tilde{\nu}}
appearing in the product must have
\nbw({\tilde{\nu}})\leq\nbw({\tilde{\pi}}|_{{\tilde{B}}})+\nbw({\tilde{\pi}}/{\tilde{B}})=\nbw({\tilde{\pi}})
with equality only if

N({\tilde{\nu}})=N({\tilde{\pi}}|_{{\tilde{B}}})\biguplus N({\tilde{\pi}}/{\tilde{B}})=N({\tilde{\pi}}).

If any vertical bars in
{\tilde{\nu}}
came from nonbasic blocks of
{\tilde{\pi}}|_{{\tilde{B}}}
and
{\tilde{\pi}}/{\tilde{B}}
meeting, then
{\tilde{\nu}}
would necessarily have a smaller nonbasic weight. Hence, in the case that
\nbw({\tilde{\nu}})=\nbw({\tilde{\pi}})
, it must either be the case that
{\tilde{\nu}}={\tilde{\pi}}
or
{\tilde{\nu}}
has fewer vertical bars. So, every
{\tilde{\nu}}\neq{\tilde{\pi}}
that appears in the product is smaller in
(\tilde{\Pi}_{2(r),k},\preceq)
.
∎

Example 7.8
.

Lemma
7.7
can be used recursively to write a diagram as a polynomial in diagrams with a single nonbasic block. At each step, the nonbasic block
{\tilde{B}}
that the diagram will next be factored at is highlighted. Notice that example
(ii)
ends where example
(i)
begins.

We now introduce our generators. For
i,j\in[k]
and
{\boldsymbol{a}}\in W_{r-1,k}
, write
P_{i,j,{\boldsymbol{a}}}
for the diagram-like basis element indexed by the set partition with singleton blocks
\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{i\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}
and
\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{\bar{j}\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}
and vertical bars whose colors have multiplicity given by
{\boldsymbol{a}}
. Now fix
i\in[r]
,
{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}\in W_{i,k}
and
{\boldsymbol{c}}\in W_{r-i,k}
. Write
R_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}
for the diagram-like basis element for the set partition with a block whose colors on top and bottom are given by
{\boldsymbol{a}}
and
{\boldsymbol{b}}
respectively as well as vertical bars with multiplicities given by
{\boldsymbol{c}}
.

Example 7.9
.

As a base case, we show how the elements
\{P_{i,j,{\boldsymbol{a}}}:i,j\in[k],{\boldsymbol{a}}\in W_{r-1,k}\}
generate the diagrams with no nonbasic blocks.

Lemma 7.10
.

The elements
\{P_{i,j,{\boldsymbol{a}}}:i,j\in[k],{\boldsymbol{a}}\in W_{r-1,k}\}
generate each
\mathcal{D}_{\tilde{\pi}}
where
{\tilde{\pi}}
has no nonbasic blocks.

Proof.

Fix
{\boldsymbol{b}}\in W_{r,k}
. For
m\leq{\boldsymbol{b}}_{1}
, write
Q_{m}
for the diagram-like basis element indexed by the multiset partition with
m
pairs of singletons
\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{1\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}
and
\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{\bar{1}\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}
along with vertical bars
\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{1,\bar{1}\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}^{{\boldsymbol{b}}_{1}-m},\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{2,\bar{2}\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}^{{\boldsymbol{b}}_{2}},\dots,\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{k,\bar{k}\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}^{{\boldsymbol{b}}_{k}}
. Notice that
Q_{1}=P_{1,1,{\boldsymbol{b}}^{\prime}}
where
{\boldsymbol{b}}^{\prime}
is
{\boldsymbol{b}}
with the first entry decremented by one.

Now consider the product
Q_{1}Q_{m}
. The singleton at the bottom of
Q_{1}
will meet one of the
m
singletons at the top of
Q_{m}
in
\frac{m}{{\boldsymbol{b}}_{1}}
of the snapshots. In the remaining snapshots, the singleton meets a vertical bar and breaks it into a singleton, resulting in
Q_{m+1}
:

Q_{1}Q_{m}=\frac{m}{{\boldsymbol{b}}_{1}}nQ_{m}+\frac{{\boldsymbol{b}}_{1}-m}{{\boldsymbol{b}}_{1}}Q_{m+1}.

Hence, the elements
Q_{m}
for
1\leq m\leq{\boldsymbol{b}}_{1}
are generated by the elements
P_{i,j,{\boldsymbol{a}}}
(see Figure
4
(i)).

Suppose
{\tilde{\pi}}
is a multiset partition with no nonbasic blocks and a singleton
\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{i\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}
with
i\neq 1
. Let
{\tilde{\pi}}^{\prime}
be the result of replacing that
\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{i\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}
with
\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{1\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}
. Then for
{\boldsymbol{c}}\in W_{r-1,k}
chosen so that
P_{i,1,{\boldsymbol{c}}}\mathcal{D}_{{\tilde{\pi}}^{\prime}}
is nonzero, this product includes
\mathcal{D}_{\tilde{\pi}}
along with diagrams with fewer vertical bars (see Figure
4
(ii)). Via this process and the corresponding process for singletons
\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{\bar{i}\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}
, we can write any basic diagram with a non-one singleton as a polynomial in diagrams with fewer non-one singletons or fewer vertical bars. Repeating this process for any diagram in the resulting polynomial with a non-one singleton terminates in a polynomial in diagrams with all basic blocks and singletons of the form
\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{1\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}
or
\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{\bar{1}\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}
. These are just the
Q_{m}
above for different choices of
{\boldsymbol{b}}
, so the
\{P_{i,j,{\boldsymbol{a}}}:i,j\in[k],{\boldsymbol{a}}\in W_{r-1,k}\}
generate the diagrams with all basic blocks.
∎

Figure 4.
Examples of the processes employed in Lemma
7.10
.

Finally, we use Lemma
7.7
and Lemma
7.10
to prove that the elements
P_{i,j,{\boldsymbol{a}}}
and
R_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}
defined above generate the algebra
{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n)
.

Theorem 7.11
.

The algebra
{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n)
is generated by the set
\Theta=\{P_{i,j,{\boldsymbol{a}}}:i,j\in[k],{\boldsymbol{a}}\in W_{r-1,k}\}\cup\{R_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}:{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}\in W_{i,k},{\boldsymbol{c}}\in W_{r-i,k}\text{ for some }i\in[r]\}
.

Proof.

If
{\tilde{\pi}}
has more than one nonbasic block, then we apply Lemma
7.7
to write
\mathcal{D}_{\tilde{\pi}}
as a polynomial in elements
\mathcal{D}_{\tilde{\nu}}
where
{\tilde{\nu}}\prec{\tilde{\pi}}
. We can iterate this process on each
\mathcal{D}_{\tilde{\nu}}
in this polynomial where
{\tilde{\nu}}
has more than one nonbasic block (see Example
7.8
). Because the poset
(\tilde{\Pi}_{2(r),k},\preceq)
is finite, this iteration terminates with
\mathcal{D}_{\tilde{\pi}}
written as a polynomial in elements
\mathcal{D}_{\tilde{\nu}}
where each
{\tilde{\nu}}
has at most one nonbasic block. Hence, it suffices to show that
\Theta
generates the elements
\mathcal{D}_{\tilde{\nu}}
where
{\tilde{\nu}}
has at most one nonbasic block.

By Lemma
7.10
,
\Theta
generates the elements
\mathcal{D}_{\tilde{\pi}}
where
{\tilde{\pi}}
has no nonbasic blocks. We now prove that
\Theta
generates the diagrams with a single nonbasic block by induction on the number of vertical bars. If
{\tilde{\pi}}
has a single nonbasic block and no vertical bars, it has a straightforward factorization as
\mathcal{D}_{\tilde{\pi}}=\mathcal{D}_{{\tilde{\pi}}_{1}}\mathcal{D}_{{\tilde{\pi}}_{2}}\mathcal{D}_{{\tilde{\pi}}_{3}}
where
{\tilde{\pi}}_{2}
is obtained from
{\tilde{\pi}}
by connecting all vertices into a single block,
{\tilde{\pi}}_{1}
has a vertical bar for each vertex at the top of the nonbasic block of
{\tilde{\pi}}
and a pair of identically colored singletons for each singleton atop
{\tilde{\pi}}
, and
{\tilde{\pi}}_{3}
is obtained similarly from the bottom of
{\tilde{\pi}}
(see Figure
5
(i)). Notice that
\mathcal{D}_{{\tilde{\pi}}_{1}},\mathcal{D}_{{\tilde{\pi}}_{2}},\mathcal{D}_{{\tilde{\pi}}_{3}}\in\Theta
.

For
{\tilde{\pi}}
with a single nonbasic block and
s
vertical bars, one can try a modified version of the above factorization in which a copy of each vertical bar in
{\tilde{\pi}}
is put in
{\tilde{\pi}}_{1}
,
{\tilde{\pi}}_{2}
, and
{\tilde{\pi}}_{3}
(see Figure
5
(ii)). The element
\mathcal{D}_{\tilde{\pi}}
appears in the product
\mathcal{D}_{{\tilde{\pi}}_{1}}\mathcal{D}_{{\tilde{\pi}}_{2}}\mathcal{D}_{{\tilde{\pi}}_{3}}
when each singleton in
{\tilde{\pi}}_{1}
and
{\tilde{\pi}}_{3}
meets the nonbasic block in
{\tilde{\pi}}_{2}
. When these singletons instead meet vertical bars in
{\tilde{\pi}}_{2}
, the resulting diagram has fewer than
s
vertical bars. By induction on the number of vertical bars, the set
\Theta
generates the diagrams with at most one nonbasic block and hence the algebra
{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(x)
.
∎
