8.
Change-of-Basis Formula

In this section, we give a change-of-basis formula from Orellana and Zabrocki’s orbit basis to the diagram-like basis. While the earlier sections dealt with the centralizer algebras
P_{r}(n)
and
{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(n)
, the combinatorics of the change-of-basis formula do not depend on the semisimplicity of the algebras. Hence, this section considers the abstract algebras
P_{r}(x)
and
{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(x)
over
\mathbb{C}(x)
for
x
an indeterminate. These results can all be applied to the centralizer algebra case by specializing
x
to an integer
n\geq 2r
.

In analogy with the construction of the diagram-like basis as a projection of the diagram basis of
P_{r}(x)
, we can define the
orbit-like basis
by projecting the orbit basis of
P_{r}(x)
:

\mathcal{O}_{{\tilde{\pi}}}=s_{\boldsymbol{a}}\mathcal{T}_{\pi}s_{\boldsymbol{b}}

where
\pi\in\Pi_{2(r)}
is any set partition so that
\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}(\pi)={\tilde{\pi}}
. For a multiset partition
{\tilde{\pi}}
, define
m_{{\tilde{B}}}({\tilde{\pi}})
to be the multiplicity of the block
{\tilde{B}}
in
{\tilde{\pi}}
and write

m({\tilde{\pi}})!=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}{\tilde{B}}\in{\tilde{\pi}}\\
\text{distinct}\end{subarray}}m_{\tilde{B}}({\tilde{\pi}})

where the product is over
distinct
blocks of
{\tilde{\pi}}
.

Theorem 8.1
.

For
{\tilde{\pi}}\in\tilde{\Pi}_{2(r),k}
whose unbarred entries have multiplicity given by
{\boldsymbol{a}}\in W_{r,k}
, write

\omega({\tilde{\pi}})=\frac{m({\tilde{\pi}})!}{\left|\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{a}}\right|}\prod_{{\tilde{B}}\in{\tilde{\pi}}}m({\tilde{B}}|_{\left[\bar{k}\right]})!.

Then the map

\displaystyle\varphi:\tilde{P}_{r,k}(x)

\displaystyle\to{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(x)

\displaystyle\mathcal{O}_{\tilde{\pi}}

\displaystyle\mapsto\omega({\tilde{\pi}})\mathcal{X}_{\tilde{\pi}}

where
\{\mathcal{X}_{\tilde{\pi}}:{\tilde{\pi}}\in\tilde{\Pi}_{2(r),k}\}
is the orbit basis of Orellana and Zabrocki is an isomorphism of algebras.

Because each
\omega({\tilde{\pi}})
is nonzero, it is clear that this map is an isomorphism of vector spaces–the remainder of this section is devoted to proving that it respects the multiplication. First, we observe that such an isomorphism gives us the following change-of-basis formula from Orellana and Zabrocki’s orbit basis to the diagram-like basis:

\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{\tilde{\pi}}

\displaystyle=\varphi(s_{\boldsymbol{a}}L_{\pi}s_{\boldsymbol{b}})

\displaystyle=\sum_{{\tilde{\nu}}\leq{\tilde{\pi}}}c_{{\tilde{\nu}},{\tilde{\pi}}}\omega({\tilde{\nu}})\mathcal{X}_{\tilde{\nu}}

where for a fixed
\pi
such that
\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}(\pi)={\tilde{\pi}}
,
c_{{\tilde{\nu}},{\tilde{\pi}}}
is the number of
\nu\leq\pi
such that
\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}(\nu)={\tilde{\nu}}
.

8.1.
Preliminary Definitions and Enumerative Results

The product formula for the orbit basis
\{\mathcal{T}_{\pi}:\pi\in\Pi_{2(r)}\}
for
P_{r}(x)
use set partitions that include unbarred, barred, and double-barred elements. To that end, we make the following definitions. For
\pi,\nu\in\Pi_{2(r)}
, write
\Gamma^{\pi}_{\nu}
for the set of set partitions
\gamma
of
[r]\cup\left[\bar{r}\right]\cup\left[\bar{\bar{r}}\right]
such that
\gamma|_{[r]\cup\left[\bar{r}\right]}=\pi
and
\gamma|_{\left[\bar{r}\right]\cup\left[\bar{\bar{r}}\right]}=\bar{\nu}
where
\bar{\nu}
is the result of adding a bar to each element in
\nu
. For such a
\gamma
, write
\beta_{\gamma}=\{S\in\gamma:\forall i\in S,i\in\left[\bar{r}\right]\}
for the set of blocks of
\gamma
containing only barred numbers. Write

b_{\gamma}(x)=(x-\ell(\gamma|_{[r]\cup\left[\bar{\bar{r}}\right]}))_{\ell(\beta_{\gamma})}

where
(a)_{n}=a(a-1)\cdots(a-n+1)
. The product formula for the orbit basis is

\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{\pi}\mathcal{T}_{\nu}

\displaystyle=\sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma^{\pi}_{\nu}}b_{\gamma}(x)\mathcal{T}_{\gamma}

where the
\gamma
in the subscript is understood to be an element of
\Pi_{2(r)}
by taking the restriction
\gamma|_{[r]\cup\left[\bar{\bar{r}}\right]}
and removing a bar from each double-barred entry (see Theorem 4.14 of
[
BH19b
]
for details).

For the orbit basis
\{\mathcal{X}_{\tilde{\pi}}:{\tilde{\pi}}\in\tilde{\Pi}_{2(r),k}\}
of
{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(x)
we make similar definitions. For
{\tilde{\pi}},{\tilde{\nu}}\in\tilde{\Pi}_{2(r),k}
, write
\tilde{\Gamma}^{\tilde{\pi}}_{\tilde{\nu}}
for the set of multiset partitions
{\tilde{\gamma}}
with
r
elements each from
[k]
,
\left[\bar{k}\right]
, and
\left[\bar{\bar{k}}\right]
such that
{\tilde{\gamma}}|_{[k]\cup\left[\bar{k}\right]}={\tilde{\pi}}
and
{\tilde{\gamma}}|_{\left[\bar{k}\right]\cup\left[\bar{\bar{k}}\right]}=\bar{{\tilde{\nu}}}
. For such a
{\tilde{\gamma}}
, write
\beta_{\tilde{\gamma}}=\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{{\tilde{S}}\in{\tilde{\gamma}}:\forall i\in{\tilde{S}},i\in\left[\bar{k}\right]\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}
. For any multiset partition
{\tilde{\rho}}
, write
m_{\tilde{S}}({\tilde{\rho}})
for the multiplicity of
{\tilde{S}}
in
{\tilde{\rho}}
and

m({\tilde{\rho}})!=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}{\tilde{S}}\in{\tilde{\rho}}\\
\text{distinct}\end{subarray}}m_{\tilde{S}}({\tilde{\rho}})!.

Finally, write

\displaystyle\tilde{b}_{\tilde{\gamma}}(x)

\displaystyle=\frac{(x-\ell({\tilde{\gamma}}|_{[k]\cup\left[\bar{\bar{k}}\right]}))_{\ell(\beta_{\tilde{\gamma}})}}{m(\beta_{\tilde{\gamma}})!}

\displaystyle a_{\tilde{\gamma}}

\displaystyle=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}{\tilde{S}}\in{\tilde{\gamma}}|_{[k]\cup\left[\bar{\bar{k}}\right]}\\
\text{distinct}\end{subarray}}\frac{\ell({\tilde{\gamma}}_{\tilde{S}})!}{m({\tilde{\gamma}}_{\tilde{S}})!}

where
{\tilde{\gamma}}_{\tilde{S}}=\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{{\tilde{T}}\in{\tilde{\gamma}}:{\tilde{T}}|_{[k]\cup\left[\bar{\bar{k}}\right]}={\tilde{S}}\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}
. Then, the product for the orbit basis of
{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(x)
is given by

\displaystyle\mathcal{X}_{\tilde{\pi}}\mathcal{X}_{\tilde{\nu}}

\displaystyle=\sum_{{\tilde{\gamma}}\in\tilde{\Gamma}^{\tilde{\pi}}_{\tilde{\nu}}}a_{\tilde{\gamma}}\tilde{b}_{\tilde{\gamma}}(x)\mathcal{X}_{\tilde{\gamma}}

where the
{\tilde{\gamma}}
in the subscript is understood to be an element of
\tilde{\Pi}_{2r,k}
by taking the restriction
\gamma|_{[k]\cup\left[\bar{\bar{k}}\right]}
and removing a bar from each double-barred entry (see Section 3 of
[
OZ23
]
for details).

To handle these set and multiset partitions on three alphabets combinatorially, we will want to extend the notation of our painting function
\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}
to them. In particular,
\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\gamma)
will be the result of replacing the unbarred, barred, and double-barred elements according to
{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}
, and
{\boldsymbol{c}}
respectively. It will be useful later to write
\Gamma_{\nu}^{\pi}({\tilde{\mu}})
for the set of
\gamma\in\Gamma_{\nu}^{\pi}
such that
\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\gamma)={\tilde{\mu}}
.

For
\pi,\nu\in\Pi_{2(r)}
with
\pi|_{\left[\bar{r}\right]}=\bar{\nu}|_{\bar{r}}
, let
\pi\ast\nu\in\Gamma^{\pi}_{\nu}
be the set partition obtained by placing the diagram of
\pi
atop the diagram of
\nu
and identifying the corresponding vertices in the center. This set partition plays a central role because any
\gamma\in\Gamma^{\pi}_{\nu}
only differs from
\pi\ast\nu
by connecting some blocks on the very top and very bottom. That is, if we denote by
\Break(\gamma)
the result of splitting each block of
\gamma
that does not contain a vertex in the middle row of the diagram into its restriction to
[r]
and restriction to
\left[\bar{r}\right]
, then
\gamma\in\Gamma^{\pi}_{\nu}
if and only if
\Break(\gamma)=\pi\ast\nu
.

To analyze the orbit basis of
{\rm M\!P\!}_{r,k}(x)
, we want to investigate how
\pi\ast\nu
acts when
\nu
is acted upon by some permutation. This inspires the definition of several subgroups of permutations. For
\rho
a set partition of
[r]
and
{\boldsymbol{a}}\in W_{r,k}
, define

\displaystyle\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{a}}^{\rho}=\{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{a}}:\sigma.\rho=\rho\}

where the action
\sigma.\rho
applies
\sigma
to each element of each block of
\rho
. This subgroup factors as a semidirect product

\displaystyle\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{a}}^{\rho}=X_{\boldsymbol{a}}^{\rho}Y_{\boldsymbol{a}}^{\rho}

where the permutations in
X_{\boldsymbol{a}}^{\rho}
permute whole blocks and the permutations in
Y_{\boldsymbol{a}}^{\rho}
permute only within blocks of
\rho
.

Example 8.4
.

For clarity, we illustrate the above factorization in the case that all elements are the same color (where the corresponding young subgroup
\mathfrak{S}_{(r)}
is equal to the full symmetric group
\mathfrak{S}_{r}
). The permutation

\sigma=(3\,4)(1\,5)(2\,6)(8)(7\,9)

fixes the set partition
\rho=\{\{1,2,4\},\{3,5,6\},\{8\},\{7,9\}\}
and hence
\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{(r)}^{\rho}
. It then factors as
\sigma=\sigma_{X}\sigma_{Y}
where

\sigma_{X}=(1\,4\,2)(3\,5\,6)(7\,9)

permutes elements within each block and

\sigma_{Y}=(1\,3)(2\,5)(4\,6)

swaps the two blocks of
\rho
of size three.

Given
\pi\in\Pi_{2(r)}
, consider the subgroup
A_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}^{\pi}
of
X_{\boldsymbol{b}}^{\pi|_{\left[\bar{r}\right]}}
that only permutes blocks in
\pi|_{\left[\bar{r}\right]}
if they are part of blocks of
\pi
that are painted identically by
\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}
(see Example
3.1
). Let
B_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}^{\nu}
be the analogous subgroup of
X_{\boldsymbol{b}}^{\nu|_{\left[\bar{r}\right]}}
for the restrictions to the top. More precisely,

\displaystyle A^{\pi}_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}

\displaystyle=\{\sigma\in X_{\boldsymbol{b}}^{\pi|_{\left[\bar{r}\right]}}:\forall S,T\in\pi,S|_{\left[\bar{r}\right]}=\sigma(T|_{\left[\bar{r}\right]})\implies\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}(S)=\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}(T)\}

\displaystyle B^{\nu}_{{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}

\displaystyle=\{\sigma\in X_{\boldsymbol{b}}^{\nu|_{[r]}}:\forall S,T\in\nu,S|_{[r]}=\sigma(T|_{[r]})\implies\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(S)=\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(T)\}

Put another way, these permutations
\sigma
of the blocks in the middle row of
\pi\ast\nu
do not change the resulting multiset partition. That is,
\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\pi\ast\nu)=\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\pi\ast\sigma.\nu)
for
\sigma\in A_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}^{\pi}
or
\sigma\in B_{{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}^{\nu}
.

Finally, we collect up formulas for the sizes of these subgroups. To that end, it will be useful to consider the following multiset partitions obtained by restricting to particular blocks.

\displaystyle{\tilde{\pi}}_{+}

\displaystyle=\{{\tilde{S}}\in{\tilde{\pi}}:\forall i\in S,i\in[k]\}

\displaystyle{\tilde{\pi}}_{-}

\displaystyle=\{{\tilde{S}}\in{\tilde{\pi}}:\forall i\in S,i\in\left[\bar{k}\right]\}

\displaystyle{\tilde{\gamma}}_{\pm}

\displaystyle=\{{\tilde{S}}\in{\tilde{\pi}}:\forall i\in S,i\in[k]\cup\left[\bar{\bar{k}}\right]\}

We think of
{\tilde{\pi}}_{+}
(resp.
{\tilde{\pi}}_{-}
) as the blocks contained entirely in the top (resp. bottom) of
{\tilde{\pi}}
and
{\tilde{\gamma}}_{\pm}
as the blocks of
{\tilde{\gamma}}
that have no vertex in the middle row.

Lemma 8.5
.

Let
{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}\in W_{r,k}
,
\pi,\nu\in\Pi_{2(r)}
,
{\tilde{\pi}}=\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}(\pi),
and
{\tilde{\nu}}=\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\nu)
. Then, the subgroups defined above have sizes given by the following.

\displaystyle\begin{array}[]{ccc}\left|X^{\rho}_{\boldsymbol{a}}\right|=m(\kappa_{\boldsymbol{a}}(\rho))!&&\left|Y^{\rho}_{\boldsymbol{a}}\right|=\prod_{{\tilde{B}}\in{\tilde{\pi}}}m({\tilde{B}}|_{\left[\bar{k}\right]})!\\
\left|A^{\pi}_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}\right|=\frac{m({\tilde{\pi}})!}{m({\tilde{\pi}}_{+})!}&&\left|B^{\nu}_{{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}\right|=\frac{m({\tilde{\nu}})!}{m({\tilde{\nu}}_{-})!}\end{array}

Furthermore, for any
{\tilde{\gamma}}\in\tilde{\Gamma}^{\tilde{\pi}}_{\tilde{\nu}}
, the size of the intersection of
A^{\pi}_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}
and
B^{\nu}_{{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}
is given by

\displaystyle\left|A^{\pi}_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}\cap B^{\nu}_{{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}\right|

\displaystyle=\frac{m({\tilde{\gamma}})!}{m({\tilde{\gamma}}_{\pm})!}.

Proof.

The equalities in the first row are clear. The next two follow from the observation that the only blocks of
{\tilde{\pi}}
that contribute to
A_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}^{\pi}
are the ones that touch the bottom, so we cancel out the contribution of those contained entirely in the top.

For the last equality, we can think of
A_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}^{\pi}\cap B^{\nu}_{{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}
as the permutations of the vertices in the middle row of
\pi\ast\nu
that only permute blocks that are the restrictions of blocks painted the same in
\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\pi\ast\nu)
. The number of such permutations is
\frac{m(\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\pi\ast\nu))!}{m(\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\pi\ast\nu)_{\pm})!}
. Because
{\tilde{\gamma}}
only differs from
\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\pi\ast\nu)
by blocks that do not touch the center (whose contributions are all canceled) we can make the substitution of
{\tilde{\gamma}}
for
\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\pi\ast\nu)
.
∎

8.2.
Proof of the Isomorphism

Proof of Theorem
8.1
.

Let
{\tilde{\pi}},{\tilde{\nu}}\in\tilde{\Pi}_{2(r)}
and let
{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{b}}^{\prime},{\boldsymbol{c}}\in W_{r,k}
be such that there exist
\pi,\nu\in\Pi_{2(r)}
so that
\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}(\pi)={\tilde{\pi}}
and
\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{b}}^{\prime},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\nu)={\tilde{\nu}}
. Note that when
{\boldsymbol{b}}\neq{\boldsymbol{b}}^{\prime}
, we have
\mathcal{O}_{\tilde{\pi}}\mathcal{O}_{\tilde{\nu}}=0
and
\mathcal{X}_{\tilde{\pi}}\mathcal{X}_{\tilde{\nu}}=0
, so we need only address the case when
{\boldsymbol{b}}={\boldsymbol{b}}^{\prime}
:

\displaystyle\mathcal{O}_{\tilde{\pi}}\mathcal{O}_{\tilde{\nu}}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\left|\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{b}}\right|}\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{b}}}s_{\boldsymbol{a}}\mathcal{T}_{\pi}\mathcal{T}_{\sigma.\nu}s_{\boldsymbol{c}}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\left|\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{b}}\right|}\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{b}}}\sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma^{\pi}_{\sigma.\nu}}b_{\gamma}(x)s_{\boldsymbol{a}}\mathcal{T}_{\gamma}s_{\boldsymbol{b}}

To simplify notation, we will write
{\tilde{\gamma}}=\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\gamma)
. Note that
b_{\gamma}(x)=\tilde{b}_{{\tilde{\gamma}}}(x)m(\beta_{\tilde{\gamma}})!
, so we can rewrite the expression as follows.

\displaystyle\mathcal{O}_{\tilde{\pi}}\mathcal{O}_{\tilde{\nu}}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\left|\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{b}}\right|}\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{b}}}\sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma^{\pi}_{\sigma.\nu}}\tilde{b}_{\tilde{\gamma}}(x)m(\beta_{\tilde{\gamma}})!\mathcal{O}_{{\tilde{\gamma}}}

We then partition the sum over the possible multiset partitions
{\tilde{\mu}}
that could arise from
\gamma
in this sum, noting that
\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\sigma.\nu)={\tilde{\nu}}
, and then we swap the order of summation to obtain

\displaystyle\mathcal{O}_{\tilde{\pi}}\mathcal{O}_{\tilde{\nu}}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\left|\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{b}}\right|}\sum_{{\tilde{\mu}}\in\tilde{\Gamma}_{{\tilde{\nu}}}^{\tilde{\pi}}}\tilde{b}_{\tilde{\mu}}(x)m(\beta_{\tilde{\mu}})!\left(\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{b}}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\gamma\in\Gamma^{\pi}_{\sigma.\nu}\\
{\tilde{\gamma}}={\tilde{\mu}}\end{subarray}}1\right)\mathcal{O}_{\tilde{\mu}}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\left|\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{b}}\right|}\sum_{{\tilde{\mu}}\in\tilde{\Gamma}_{{\tilde{\nu}}}^{\tilde{\pi}}}\tilde{b}_{\tilde{\mu}}(x)m(\beta_{\tilde{\mu}})!\left(\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{b}}}\left|\Gamma^{\pi}_{\sigma.\nu}({\tilde{\mu}})\right|\right)\mathcal{O}_{\tilde{\mu}}.

Recall that
\varphi(\mathcal{O}_{\tilde{\pi}})=\omega({\tilde{\pi}})X_{\tilde{\pi}}
. Applying
\varphi
to both sides of the above equation and writing
\varphi(\mathcal{O}_{\tilde{\pi}}\mathcal{O}_{\tilde{\nu}})|_{\mathcal{X}_{\tilde{\tau}}}
for the coefficient of
\mathcal{X}_{\tilde{\tau}}
in
\varphi(\mathcal{O}_{\tilde{\pi}}\mathcal{O}_{\tilde{\nu}})
then yields

(6)

\displaystyle\varphi(\mathcal{O}_{\tilde{\pi}}\mathcal{O}_{\tilde{\nu}})|_{\mathcal{X}_{\tilde{\tau}}}

\displaystyle=\frac{\omega({\tilde{\tau}})}{\left|\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{b}}\right|}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}{\tilde{\mu}}\in\Gamma^{\tilde{\pi}}_{\tilde{\nu}}\\
{\tilde{\mu}}|_{[k]\cup\left[\bar{\bar{k}}\right]}={\tilde{\tau}}\end{subarray}}\tilde{b}_{\tilde{\mu}}(x)m(\beta_{\tilde{\mu}})!\left(\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{b}}}\left|\Gamma^{\pi}_{\sigma.\nu}({\tilde{\mu}})\right|\right).

We now compare this to the same coefficient in
\varphi(\mathcal{O}_{\tilde{\pi}})\varphi(\mathcal{O}_{\tilde{\nu}})
:

(7)

\displaystyle\varphi(\mathcal{O}_{\tilde{\pi}})\varphi(\mathcal{O}_{\tilde{\nu}})|_{\mathcal{X}_{\tilde{\tau}}}

\displaystyle=\omega({\tilde{\pi}})\omega({\tilde{\nu}})\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}{\tilde{\mu}}\in\tilde{\Gamma}^{\tilde{\pi}}_{\tilde{\nu}}\\
{\tilde{\mu}}|_{[k]\cup\left[\bar{\bar{k}}\right]={\tilde{\tau}}}\end{subarray}}a_{\tilde{\mu}}\tilde{b}_{\tilde{\mu}}(x)

The goal is now to show that the rather unpleasant expressions given in Equation
6
for
\varphi(\mathcal{O}_{\tilde{\pi}}\mathcal{O}_{\tilde{\nu}})
and Equation
7
for
\varphi(\mathcal{O}_{\tilde{\pi}})\varphi(\mathcal{O}_{\tilde{\nu}})
are equal. We will leverage their similarities—namely that they sum over the same objects and each include a factor of
\tilde{b}_{\tilde{\mu}}(x)
in each summand—to simplify the task. It would suffice to show the following equality:

\displaystyle\frac{\omega({\tilde{\tau}})}{\left|\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{b}}\right|}m(\beta_{\tilde{\mu}})!\left(\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{b}}}\left|\Gamma^{\pi}_{\sigma.\nu}({\tilde{\mu}})\right|\right)

\displaystyle=\omega({\tilde{\pi}})\omega({\tilde{\nu}})a_{\tilde{\mu}}

By using the definition of
\omega({\tilde{\pi}})
and noticing that
{\tilde{\tau}}|_{\left[\bar{k}\right]}={\tilde{\nu}}|_{\left[\bar{k}\right]}
, we are able to rearrange the above equality to

\displaystyle\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{b}}}\left|\Gamma^{\pi}_{\sigma.\nu}({\tilde{\mu}})\right|

\displaystyle=a_{\tilde{\mu}}\frac{m({\tilde{\pi}})!m({\tilde{\nu}})!}{m({\tilde{\tau}})!m(\beta_{\tilde{\mu}})!}\prod_{{\tilde{B}}\in{\tilde{\pi}}}m({\tilde{B}}|_{\left[\bar{k}\right]})!.

Then using the formulas in Lemma
8.5
for the sizes of the subgroups, we rewrite the right-hand side to obtain

\displaystyle\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{b}}}\left|\Gamma^{\pi}_{\sigma.\nu}({\tilde{\mu}})\right|

\displaystyle=a_{\tilde{\mu}}\frac{m({\tilde{\pi}}_{+})!m({\tilde{\nu}}_{-})!}{m({\tilde{\tau}})!m(\beta_{\tilde{\mu}})!}\frac{m({\tilde{\mu}})!}{m({\tilde{\mu}}_{\pm})!}\frac{\left|A^{\pi}_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}\right|\left|B^{\nu}_{{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}\right|\left|Y_{\boldsymbol{b}}^{\pi|_{\left[\bar{r}\right]}}\right|}{\left|A_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}^{\pi}\cap B_{{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}^{\nu}\right|}

\displaystyle=a_{\tilde{\mu}}\frac{m({\tilde{\pi}}_{+})!m({\tilde{\nu}}_{-})!}{m({\tilde{\tau}})!m(\beta_{\tilde{\mu}})!}\frac{m({\tilde{\mu}})!}{m({\tilde{\mu}}_{\pm})!}\left|A_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}^{\pi}B_{{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}^{\nu}Y_{\boldsymbol{b}}^{\pi|_{\left[\bar{r}\right]}}\right|

\displaystyle=\left(a_{\tilde{\mu}}\frac{m({\tilde{\mu}})!}{m({\tilde{\tau}})!m(\beta_{\tilde{\mu}})!}\right)\frac{m({\tilde{\pi}}_{+})!m({\tilde{\nu}}_{-})!}{m({\tilde{\mu}}_{\pm})!}

where the second equality follows from the fact that
A_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}^{\pi}
and
B_{{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}^{\nu}
are subgroups of
X_{\boldsymbol{b}}^{\pi|_{\left[\bar{r}\right]}}
, which intersects trivially with
Y_{\boldsymbol{b}}^{\pi|_{\left[\bar{r}\right]}}
.

Finally, we turn our attention to the factor in parentheses in the above expression. Because
{\tilde{\tau}}={\tilde{\mu}}|_{\left[\bar{k}\right]\cup\left[\bar{\bar{k}}\right]}
, we have for each block
{\tilde{S}}\in{\tilde{\mu}}|_{\left[\bar{k}\right]\cup\left[\bar{\bar{k}}\right]}
that
\ell({\tilde{\mu}}_{{\tilde{S}}})=m_{{\tilde{S}}}({\tilde{\tau}})
. This fact allows us to cancel the
\ell({\tilde{\mu}}_{\tilde{S}})!
terms in the definition of
a_{\tilde{\mu}}
with
m({\tilde{\tau}})!
to get

\displaystyle a_{\tilde{\mu}}\frac{m({\tilde{\mu}})!}{m({\tilde{\tau}})!m(\beta_{\tilde{\mu}})!}

\displaystyle=\left(\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}{\tilde{S}}\in{\tilde{\mu}}|_{[k]\cup\left[\bar{\bar{k}}\right]}\\
\text{distinct}\end{subarray}}\frac{\ell({\tilde{\mu}}_{\tilde{S}})!}{m({\tilde{\mu}}_{\tilde{S}})!}\right)\frac{m({\tilde{\mu}})!}{m({\tilde{\tau}})!m(\beta_{\tilde{\mu}})!}

\displaystyle=\left(\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}{\tilde{S}}\in{\tilde{\mu}}|_{[k]\cup\left[\bar{\bar{k}}\right]}\\
\text{distinct}\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{m({\tilde{\mu}}_{\tilde{S}})!}\right)\frac{m({\tilde{\mu}})!}{m(\beta_{\tilde{\mu}})!}.

Note that the terms
m({\tilde{\mu}}_{\tilde{S}})!
contribute
m_{\tilde{U}}({\tilde{\mu}})!
to the denominator for each block
{\tilde{U}}\in{\tilde{\mu}}
which contains either an unbarred or a double-barred element. Furthermore,
m(\beta_{\tilde{\mu}})!
contributes a
m_{\tilde{U}}({\tilde{\mu}})!
to the denominator for each block
{\tilde{U}}\in{\tilde{\mu}}
consisting only of barred elements. In total, this cancels the contribution of
m({\tilde{\mu}})!
, so

\displaystyle a_{\tilde{\mu}}\frac{m({\tilde{\mu}})!}{m({\tilde{\tau}})!m(\beta_{\tilde{\mu}})!}

\displaystyle=1

Hence,
\varphi
is an isomorphism of algebras if the equality

\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{b}}}\left|\Gamma^{\pi}_{\sigma.\nu}({\tilde{\mu}})\right|=\frac{m({\tilde{\pi}}_{+})m({\tilde{\nu}}_{-})}{m({\tilde{\mu}}_{\pm})}{\left|A_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}^{\pi}B_{{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}^{\nu}Y_{{\boldsymbol{b}}}^{\pi|_{\left[\bar{r}\right]}}\right|}

holds. The proof of this equality will be carried out in two lemmas. First, Lemma
8.8
will show that the set of
\sigma
such that
\left|\Gamma_{\sigma.\nu}^{\pi}({\tilde{\mu}})\right|\neq 0
is given by a translation of the product
A_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}^{\pi}B_{{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}^{\nu^{\prime}}Y_{\boldsymbol{b}}^{\pi|_{\left[\bar{r}\right]}}
where
\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\nu^{\prime})=\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\nu)
so
B_{{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}^{\nu^{\prime}}\cong B_{{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}^{\nu}
. Finally, Lemma
8.11
will show that for each such
\sigma
,

\displaystyle\left|\Gamma_{\sigma.\nu}^{\pi}({\tilde{\mu}})\right|=\frac{m_{+}({\tilde{\pi}})m_{-}({\tilde{\nu}})}{m_{\pm}({\tilde{\mu}})}.

Because this quantity is independent of
\sigma
, the value of the sum is simply the product of the quantity
\frac{m_{+}({\tilde{\pi}})m_{-}({\tilde{\nu}})}{m_{\pm}({\tilde{\mu}})}
with the number of nonzero summands, given by
\left|A_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}^{\pi}B_{{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}^{\nu^{\prime}}Y_{\boldsymbol{b}}^{\pi|_{\left[\bar{r}\right]}}\right|
.
∎

To set the stage for the final two lemmas, we first need to investigate a particular class of permutations in
\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{b}}^{\rho}
.

Lemma 8.6
.

Let
\pi,\nu\in\Pi_{2(r)}
such that
\pi|_{\left[\bar{r}\right]}=\bar{\nu}|_{\left[\bar{r}\right]}=\rho
and fix
{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}\in W_{r,k}
. Then

\{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{b}}^{\rho}:\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\pi\ast\sigma.\nu)=\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\pi\ast\nu)\}=A_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}^{\pi}B_{{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}^{\nu}Y_{{\boldsymbol{b}}}^{\rho}.

Proof.

First, note that
\sigma
factors as
\sigma=\sigma_{X}\sigma_{Y}
for
\sigma_{X}\in X_{\boldsymbol{m}}^{\rho}
and
\sigma_{Y}\in Y_{\boldsymbol{m}}^{\rho}
. Because
\sigma_{Y}.\nu=\nu
for all
\nu
, we need only determine which
\sigma_{X}
can be factored into a product of an element of
A_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}^{\pi}
and an element of
B_{{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}^{\nu}
.

One containment is straightforward. Suppose
\sigma_{X}=\sigma_{A}\sigma_{B}
with
\sigma_{A}\in A_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}^{\pi}
and
\sigma_{B}\in B_{{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}^{\nu}
. Consider a block in
\pi\ast\nu
. Although the bottom half of this block may be different in
\pi\ast\sigma_{B}.\nu
, the condition that
\sigma_{B}\in B_{{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}^{\nu}
guarantees that it is not different in
\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\pi\ast\sigma_{B}.\nu)
. Hence,
\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\pi\ast\sigma_{B}.\nu)=\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\pi\ast\nu)
for any
\pi\in\Pi_{2(r)}
with
\pi|_{\left[\bar{r}\right]}=\bar{\nu}|_{\left[\bar{r}\right]}
. Analogously, we see that
\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\pi.{\sigma_{A}}^{-1}\ast\nu)=\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\pi\ast\nu)
for any
\nu\in\Pi_{2(r)}
with
\pi|_{\left[\bar{r}\right]}=\bar{\nu}|_{\left[\bar{r}\right]}
. Hence,

\displaystyle\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\pi\ast\sigma_{A}\sigma_{B}.\nu)

\displaystyle=\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\pi.{\sigma_{A}}^{-1}\ast\sigma_{B}.\nu)

\displaystyle=\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\pi.{\sigma_{A}}^{-1}\ast\nu)

\displaystyle=\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\pi\ast\nu).

For the other containment, suppose that
\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\pi\ast\nu)=\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\pi\ast\sigma_{X}.\nu)={\tilde{\mu}}
. We use the following convention for indexing the blocks of
\pi\ast\nu
. Write
\rho=\{M_{1}<\dots<M_{\ell}\}
for the restrictions of the blocks of
\pi\ast\nu
to
\left[\bar{r}\right]
in last-letter order, and write
S_{i}
for the block of
\pi\ast\nu
with
M_{i}\subseteq S_{i}
. An element
\sigma\in X_{\boldsymbol{m}}^{\rho}
permutes the blocks of
\rho
and hence the indices
[\ell]
. For
S_{i}\in\pi\ast\nu
, it will be helpful to write
\sigma(S_{i})
for the block in
\pi\ast\sigma.\nu
such that
S_{i}|_{[r]\cup\left[\bar{r}\right]}=\sigma(S_{i})|_{[r]\cup\left[\bar{r}\right]}
. Equivalently,
\sigma(S_{i})
is obtained by replacing the bottom row
S_{i}|_{\left[\bar{\bar{r}}\right]}
with
S_{\sigma^{-1}(i)}|_{\left[\bar{\bar{r}}\right]}
.

For a fixed
\sigma\in X_{\boldsymbol{b}}^{\rho}
and
{\tilde{S}}
a multiset from
[k]\cup\left[\bar{k}\right]\cup\left[\bar{\bar{k}}\right]
, write

W_{\sigma,{\tilde{S}}}=\{i:\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\sigma(S_{i}))={\tilde{S}}\}.

For an example of these sets, see Example
8.7
. The following two properties can be observed in this example—we show that they hold in general.

1.

For a fixed
{\tilde{R}}\in\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}(\pi)
such that
{\tilde{R}}\cap\left[\bar{k}\right]\neq\emptyset
,

\displaystyle\biguplus_{\begin{subarray}{c}{\tilde{S}}\in{\tilde{\mu}}\\
{\tilde{S}}|_{[k]\cup\left[\bar{k}\right]}={\tilde{R}}\end{subarray}}W_{1,{\tilde{S}}}=\biguplus_{\begin{subarray}{c}{\tilde{S}}\in{\tilde{\mu}}\\
{\tilde{S}}|_{[k]\cup\left[\bar{k}\right]}={\tilde{R}}\end{subarray}}W_{\sigma_{X},{\tilde{S}}}.

This follows just about immediately from the fact that
\sigma(S_{i})|_{[r]\cup\left[\bar{r}\right]}=S_{i}|_{[r]\cup\left[\bar{r}\right]}
for any
\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{b}}^{\rho}
. Furthermore,

\displaystyle\biguplus_{\begin{subarray}{c}{\tilde{S}}\in{\tilde{\mu}}\\
{\tilde{S}}|_{[k]\cup\left[\bar{k}\right]}={\tilde{R}}\end{subarray}}W_{\sigma_{X},{\tilde{S}}}

\displaystyle=\left\{i:\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\sigma_{X}(S_{i}))|_{[k]\cup\left[\bar{k}\right]}={\tilde{R}}\right\}

\displaystyle=\left\{i:\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(S_{i})|_{[k]\cup\left[\bar{k}\right]}={\tilde{R}}\right\}

\displaystyle=\biguplus_{\begin{subarray}{c}{\tilde{S}}\in{\tilde{\mu}}\\
{\tilde{S}}|_{[k]\cup\left[\bar{k}\right]}={\tilde{R}}\end{subarray}}W_{1,{\tilde{S}}}.

Note that the assumption that
\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\pi\ast\nu)=\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\pi\ast\sigma_{X}.\nu)={\tilde{\mu}}
is necessary here so that the unions on either side of the equality are over the same set of
{\tilde{S}}
.

2.

For a fixed
{\tilde{S}}\in{\tilde{\mu}}
with
{\tilde{S}}\cap\left[\bar{k}\right]\neq\emptyset
,

\displaystyle|W_{\sigma_{X},{\tilde{S}}}|=|W_{1,{\tilde{S}}}|.

For
\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{b}}^{\rho}
and
{\tilde{S}}\in\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\pi\ast\sigma.\nu)
with
{\tilde{S}}\cap\left[\bar{k}\right]\neq\emptyset
, we have

\displaystyle\left|W_{\sigma,{\tilde{S}}}\right|

\displaystyle=\left|\left\{i:\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\sigma(S_{i}))={\tilde{S}}\right\}\right|

\displaystyle=m_{{\tilde{S}}}(\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\pi\ast\sigma.\nu)).

The statement then follows from the assumption that
\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\pi\ast\nu)=\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\pi\ast\sigma_{X}.\nu)={\tilde{\mu}}
.

These two facts allow us to construct a permutation in the following way. Fixing
{\tilde{R}}\in\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}(\pi)
such that
{\tilde{R}}\cap\left[\bar{k}\right]\neq\emptyset
, there exists a permutation
\eta_{{\tilde{R}}}
of
\{i:\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(S_{i})|_{[k]\cup\left[\bar{k}\right]}={\tilde{R}}\}
such that
\eta_{\tilde{R}}(W_{\sigma_{X},{\tilde{S}}})=W_{1,{\tilde{S}}}
for all
{\tilde{S}}
with
{\tilde{S}}|_{[k]\cup\left[\bar{k}\right]}={\tilde{R}}
. Because
\eta_{\tilde{R}}
by definition permutes only blocks that restrict to the same block in
\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}(\pi)
, we see
\eta_{\tilde{R}}
is an element of
A_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}^{\pi}
. Now define
\eta\in A_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}^{\pi}
by

\displaystyle\eta:=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}{\tilde{R}}\in\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}(\pi)\\
{\tilde{R}}\cap\left[\bar{k}\right]\neq\emptyset\end{subarray}}\eta_{\tilde{R}}

with the product taken in any order.

It remains only to show that
\eta\sigma_{X}\in B_{{\boldsymbol{m}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}^{\nu}
. Fix
i\in[\ell]
and let
{\tilde{S}}=\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\eta\sigma_{X}(S_{i}))
. Then,

\displaystyle{\tilde{S}}

\displaystyle=\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\eta\sigma_{X}(S_{i}))

\displaystyle=\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}(S_{i}|_{[r]\cup\left[\bar{r}\right]})\cup\kappa_{\boldsymbol{c}}(S_{(\eta\sigma_{X})^{-1}(i)}).

Then by the fact that
\eta\in A_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}^{\pi}
,

\displaystyle{\tilde{S}}

\displaystyle=\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}(S_{\eta^{-1}(i)}|_{[r]\cup\left[\bar{r}\right]})\cup\kappa_{\boldsymbol{c}}(S_{{\sigma_{X}}^{-1}(\eta^{-1}(i))})

\displaystyle=\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\sigma_{X}(S_{\eta^{-1}(i)})).

Then
\eta^{-1}(i)\in W_{\sigma_{X},{\tilde{S}}}
, so
i\in\eta(W_{\sigma_{X},{\tilde{S}}})=W_{1,{\tilde{S}}}
. Hence,
{\tilde{S}}_{i}={\tilde{S}}=\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\eta\sigma_{X}(S_{i}))
for each
i
and so
\eta\sigma_{X}\in B^{\pi}_{{\boldsymbol{t}},{\boldsymbol{m}}}
, meaning
\sigma_{X}\in A_{{\boldsymbol{t}},{\boldsymbol{m}}}^{\pi}B_{{\boldsymbol{m}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}^{\nu}
. Thus
\sigma=\sigma_{X}\sigma_{Y}\in A_{{\boldsymbol{t}},{\boldsymbol{m}}}^{\pi}B_{{\boldsymbol{m}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}^{\nu}Y_{\boldsymbol{m}}^{\rho}
.
∎

.

defined in Lemma
8.6
. This definition relies on an (arbitrary) ordering of the blocks of
\pi\ast\nu
which contain a barred element (i.e. touch the middle row in the diagram). In this example, we order these blocks by their restriction to the middle row, and we label them as-such in the following diagram.

Now we can read off that
\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\sigma_{X}(S_{2}))=\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{1,1,\bar{1},\bar{2},\bar{\bar{1}}\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}
by looking at the block labeled
2
in the above diagram.

Consider
{\tilde{R}}=\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{1,\bar{2}\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}\in\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}(\pi)
. There are two distinct blocks in
\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\pi\ast\nu)
that restrict to this
{\tilde{R}}
:
{\tilde{S}}=\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{1,\bar{2},\bar{\bar{2}},\bar{\bar{2}}\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}
and
{\tilde{S}}^{\prime}=\left\{\mskip-5.0mu\left\{1,\bar{2},\bar{\bar{3}}\right\}\mskip-5.0mu\right\}
. The first corresponds to the blocks labeled
3
and
4
, while the second corresponds to just the block labeled
5
. From this, we can conclude the following:

\displaystyle W_{1,{\tilde{S}}}=\{3,4\}

\displaystyle W_{1,{\tilde{S}}^{\prime}}=\{5\}

Applying the same logic to
\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\pi\ast\nu)
yields the following:

\displaystyle W_{\sigma_{X},{\tilde{S}}}=\{4,5\}

\displaystyle W_{\sigma_{X},{\tilde{S}}^{\prime}}=\{3\}

Notice that the sets in each column have the same size and the union across rows is always
\{3,4,5\}
.

Lemma 8.8
.

Fix
\pi,\nu\in\Pi_{2(r)}
such that
\pi|_{\left[\bar{r}\right]}=\bar{\nu}_{\left[\bar{r}\right]}=\rho
and
{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}\in W_{r,k}
. Let
{\tilde{\mu}}\in\tilde{\Gamma}_{\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\nu)}^{\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}(\pi)}
. The set of
\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{m}}
for which there exists a
\gamma\in\Gamma_{\sigma.\nu}^{\pi}({\tilde{\mu}})
is given by

\displaystyle A_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}^{\pi}B_{{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}^{\sigma_{0}.\nu}Y_{\boldsymbol{b}}^{\rho}\sigma_{0}

for some
\sigma_{0}\in\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{b}}
.

Proof.

Let
\pi,\nu\in\Pi_{2(r)}
. If there exists
\gamma\in\Gamma^{\pi}_{\nu}({\tilde{\mu}})
, then

\Break({\tilde{\mu}})=\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\pi\ast\nu).

Conversely if
\Break({\tilde{\mu}})=\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\pi\ast\nu)
we can construct a
\gamma\in\Gamma_{\nu}^{\pi}({\tilde{\mu}})
as follows. For each block of
{\tilde{\mu}}
broken into
\tilde{T}
in the top and
\tilde{B}
in the bottom, find blocks
T
and
B
in
\pi
and
\nu
for which
\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}(T)=\tilde{T}
and
\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(B)=\tilde{B}
and connect these blocks in
\pi\ast\nu
. After connecting such a pair for each block broken in
\mu
, we have constructed the desired
\gamma
(see Example
8.9
).

Hence, we are looking for the set of
\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{b}}
for which
\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\pi\ast\sigma.\nu)=\Break({\tilde{\mu}})
. Note that
\pi\ast\sigma.\nu
only makes sense when
\sigma.\nu|_{[r]}=\rho
, so we need only consider
\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{b}}^{\rho}
.

Choose
\sigma_{0}
so that
\Break({\tilde{\mu}})=\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\pi\ast\sigma_{0}.\nu)
and write
\nu^{\prime}=\sigma_{0}.\nu
. Then the desired set of
\sigma
is precisely the permutations
\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{m}}^{\rho}
such that

\displaystyle\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\pi\ast(\sigma\sigma_{0}^{-1}).\nu^{\prime})=\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\pi\ast\nu^{\prime}).

Lemma
8.6
tells us that this set is precisely those
\sigma
where

\displaystyle\sigma{\sigma_{0}}^{-1}\in A_{{\boldsymbol{t}},{\boldsymbol{m}}}^{\pi}B_{{\boldsymbol{m}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}^{\nu^{\prime}}Y_{\boldsymbol{m}}^{\rho}

as desired.

∎

Lemma 8.10
.

Let
\mu
be a set partition of
[m]
and
{\boldsymbol{a}}\in W_{m,\ell}
such that the blocks of
\kappa_{\boldsymbol{a}}(\mu)={\tilde{\mu}}
are all sets. Then the number of set partitions
\gamma
of
[m]
such that
\kappa_{\boldsymbol{a}}(\gamma)={\tilde{\mu}}
is

\displaystyle\frac{{\boldsymbol{a}}_{1}!\dots{\boldsymbol{a}}_{\ell}!}{m({\tilde{\mu}})!}.

Proof.

First, observe that

\displaystyle\{\gamma:\kappa_{\boldsymbol{a}}(\gamma)={\tilde{\mu}}\}=\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{a}}.\mu.

By the orbit-stabilizer theorem (see
[
Art91
, Proposition 6.8.4]
), the size of this orbit is the same as the number of cosets of the corresponding stabilizer
\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{a}}^{\mu}
. Because the blocks of
{\tilde{\mu}}
are sets, no permutation of
\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{a}}
swaps elements within a block of
\mu
. Hence, the permutations that fix
\mu
are precisely the ones that swap whole blocks, so
\left|\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{a}}^{\mu}\right|=m({\tilde{\mu}})!
. The number of cosets is then obtained using Lagrange’s theorem as the quotient of
\left|\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{a}}\right|
by the size of this stabilizer.
∎

Lemma 8.11
.

Fix
\pi,\nu\in\Pi_{2(r)}
and suppose
{\tilde{\mu}}\in\tilde{\Gamma}^{\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}({\tilde{\pi}})}_{\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}({\tilde{\nu}})}
. If
\Gamma_{\nu}^{\pi}({\tilde{\mu}})\neq\emptyset
, then

\left|\Gamma^{\pi}_{\nu}({\tilde{\mu}})\right|=\frac{m({\tilde{\pi}}_{+})!m({\tilde{\nu}}_{-})!}{m({\tilde{\mu}}_{\pm})!}.

Proof.

Let
\gamma\in\Gamma_{\nu}^{\pi}({\tilde{\mu}})
. Because
\gamma
differs from
\pi\ast\nu
by connecting some number of blocks in the very top and very bottom, we can recover
\gamma
uniquely from the partial matching of blocks of
(\pi\ast\nu)_{\pm}
induced by
\gamma_{\pm}
. The question then becomes how many set partitions
\rho
on the blocks of
(\pi\ast\nu)_{\pm}
there are such that
\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\rho)={\tilde{\mu}}_{\pm}
. Because we are only connecting blocks on top to blocks on bottom, we can apply Lemma
8.10
where the
\ell
colors are the different multisets that appear in
{\tilde{\mu}}_{\pm}
. The number is then

\displaystyle\frac{m({\tilde{\mu}}_{\pm}|_{[k]})!m({\tilde{\mu}}_{\pm}|_{\left[\bar{\bar{k}}\right]})!}{m({\tilde{\mu}}_{\pm})!}

\displaystyle=\frac{m({\tilde{\pi}}_{+})!m(\nu_{-})!}{m({\tilde{\mu}}_{\pm})!}

where
{\tilde{\pi}}=\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{a}},{\boldsymbol{b}}}(\pi)
and
{\tilde{\nu}}=\kappa_{{\boldsymbol{b}},{\boldsymbol{c}}}(\nu)
.
∎
